chapters.summary: Chair Hudson introduces herself, states her pronouns, welcomes attendees to the hearing on shelter safety, and recognizes Council Members Morano, Ung, and Wilson.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson opens shelter safety hearing and introduces members

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm Crystal Hudson, chair of the New York City Council's General Welfare Committee, and my pronouns are she, her.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all for joining us for today's hearing on shelter safety.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We are additionally joined by council members Murano, Ung, and Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought there was somebody else over there.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Every New Yorker deserves a safe place to live, including New Yorkers who turn to the city for shelter during a period of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Shelter must be more than a roof over someone's head.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It must be a place where people can rest without fear of violence, access the support they need, and be treated with respect.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: However, we have heard too many concerns about conditions that can make shelters unsafe, including deteriorating facilities, overcrowding, violence, theft, and insufficient staffing.

chapters.summary: Hudson says shelter must be safe and dignified, citing deteriorating facilities, overcrowding, violence, theft, and understaffing. She notes over 83,000 people slept in shelters and over 500 sites, mostly nonprofit-run.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson outlines shelter safety concerns and system growth

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: When people feel that entering a shelter puts their safety, security,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: or dignity at risk, they may choose not to enter shelter at all.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Some of the major safety issues we will look at today include not just security incidents such as arrests, thefts, or violence, but also how the shelter

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: systems design can impact physical and mental health and well-being, exacerbate trauma, and deter New Yorkers from engaging with our shelter system and making use of the robust social safety net DSS can provide.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The New York City shelter system is sprawling.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In the 1980s, a series of lawsuits resulted in the establishment of a right to shelter in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: This was an incredibly important step towards serving unhoused New Yorkers and resulted in the city needing to increase shelter capacity.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Over the last 40 years, the number of shelters and the shelter population has grown.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Just this past Sunday, over 83,000 individuals slept in our shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Today, there are over 500 shelters throughout the city that serve single adults, adult families, and families with children.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The majority of shelters are operated by contracted nonprofit organizations.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And while most of these organizations are dedicated to serving New Yorkers, third-party contracting can result in oversight and compliance challenges, including sometimes funding unscrupulous actors, subsidizing exorbitant executive salaries,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: or inadvertently developing contracts that force providers to focus more on volume than long-term success.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: sustainable outcomes, and client well-being.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Further, the additional layer of administration can make it difficult for providers to make essential repairs or changes to premises that improve safety and security.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Last week at our joint hearing with the Committee on Veterans, for example, we heard about the difficult and lengthy process for making essential repairs to the Borden Avenue Veterans residents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Resulting in a multi-year process to repair a leaking roof.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Today's hearing is an opportunity to hear from DSS about how they address shelter safety concerns, conduct oversight of challenges to shelter safety, and to hear from the public about what the city can do better.

chapters.summary: Hudson says the hearing will examine DSS oversight and two bills: Intro 99 on family shelter placements and Intro 387 on critical incident reporting.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson previews Intro 99 and Intro 387

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In addition to today's oversight on shelter safety,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We will also consider two bills intended to strengthen transparency and accountability in the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Introduction 99, sponsored by Councilmember Gail Brewer, would require the Department of Homeless Services to report annually on the number of families with children placed in shelters in the same or an adjoining zip code as their last address.

chapters.summary: Brewer says Intro 99 would require DHS to report annually on families with children placed in the same or an adjoining zip code as their last address, to keep children near schools and support networks.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer explains Intro 99 on family shelter placements

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer, I now pass to you to make a statement about the legislation you're sponsoring today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 99, as you heard earlier, would require the Department of Homeless Services to do this annual report on the number and percentage of families with children in the system who are placed in the same zip

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: code as their last address prior to their placement into a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the number and percentage who were placed in an adjoining zip code.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Families entering the shelter system, as you know, should be able to remain close to their schools, their child care, their doctors, their jobs, and their community support networks whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Placing families far from their former homes creates additional hardships, particularly for families with young children who rely on nearby child care and family support.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We in the council and the public need to know how often families are placed in shelters in their former zip code or an adjoining zip code.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Currently, this information is not regularly reported.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 99 requires DHS to report annually on shelter placements with data broken down by borough and by families with children under age three and those with older children.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I believe that this reporting will help the council identify where families are being displaced from their communities and push for shelter placement policies that minimize disruption to children's lives.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I must admit during the

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: issue when we had so many wonderful migrants here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I really appreciated the work that the Adams administration did despite all the challenges and housing people.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: With DSS at the time, we worked really hard to keep, if people move shelters, to keep them in their school zone.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: based on all of this criteria to remain close, schools are the most important.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I want this bill particularly to try to keep the families near their schools, absenteeism, a DLE, or whatever the hell it's called now, New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is huge and I have a horrible feeling that part of it is because people just can't get to school.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I also always want to thank Wynn for their support.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Hudson says Intro 387, sponsored by the Public Advocate, would require annual reporting on critical incidents, security improvements, and NYPD agreements.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson introduces Intro 387 on critical incident reporting

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro number 387, sponsored by the Public Advocate, would require annual reporting on critical incidents in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It would also require information about efforts to improve shelter security and agreements with the NYPD or other entities to enhance safety.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I now pass to the public advocate to make a statement about the legislation he's sponsoring today.

chapters.summary: Williams says 83,000 people are in shelter, cites Priority 1 incidents at a women's shelter, and argues Intro 387 would improve reporting on assaults, weapons, arson, and theft.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams testifies on Intro 387 and shelter safety data

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As I mentioned, my name is Jermaine Williams, Public Advocate of the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: More importantly, the Knicks won a game last night.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm very excited about that.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Hudson and the members of the Committee on General Welfare for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As of October 2026, a total of 83,000 individuals reside within our city's shelter system, including 51,000 families with children.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Countless others brave the harsh elements outside, deterred by unsafe conditions in these shelters.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 387, will require the Department of Homeless Services, DHS, to produce an annual report detailing critical incidents occurring in the shelters, including assault, sexual assault, dementia,

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: domestic violence, child abuse or neglect, weapons possession, arson, and theft.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is my hope that with more accurate reporting, efforts to upgrade security and shelters and enhance people's safety and well-being will be

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: more well-informed and overall more effective as the bill will require the details be shared about agreements made between DHS, the New York City Police Department, NYPD, and other entities responsible for safety and security.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Under current reporting, DHS officials have classified Priority 1 incidents as the most serious incidents involving assaults, arrests, medical crisis, overdoses, and deaths.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In one women's shelter, Priority 1 incidents have increased drastically, rising from 123 in 2019 to 208 in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2025, the rate of priority ones at this facility were over double the citywide average for single adult shelters.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: While the rate and severity of incidents may vary across shelters, trends of violence hold true across the system, especially at larger shelter sites.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Bellevue.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The city's largest shelter for single adult men, which closed earlier this year for redevelopment, was also characterized, unfortunately, by violence.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also want to uplift the other piece of legislation being heard today for which I'm proud to co-sponsor, Councilmember Brewer's Intro 99, which she just spoke about, would require DHS to report on the placement of families with children and shelters, specifically the rate of families and children who are placed within

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: the same or in adjoining zip codes as their last address prior to shelter placement.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Displacement from one's home is already a

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: source of significant stress and emotional upheaval for families, but placement in neighborhoods nearby would avoid disrupting children's school lives and routines, adding an additional layer of uncertainty and rest.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This data will better help us understand what happens when families enter the system and how we can better mitigate disruption in the lives of our youngest New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As the administration seeks to revamp the shelter system following this cold snap of last year, we must ensure that New Yorkers experiencing homelessness not only have access to shelter, but to spaces that are safe and truly livable.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These bills are one step towards ensuring safety and security within shelters.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I look forward to continuing the work with the agencies in this administration.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Hudson thanks committee and personal staff, then introduces a panel of people with shelter experience: Denton Hutchinson, Janet Jackson, and Francisco Insfran.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson thanks staff and introduces first public panel

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration and the public about these proposals.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I'd like to conclude by thanking the committee staff for their work on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Hannah Cohn, Penina Rosenberg, Justin Campos, Farida Rahman, Elizabeth Childers-Garcia, Julia Haramis, Colby Porter, and Maggie Giordano.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my staff, Andrew Wright, Elika Runtan, and Demi Brown.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Before we hear testimony from the administration, we will hear directly from a panel of individuals who have experience with New York City shelters and who have joined us here to provide testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So first, we will hear from Denton Hutchinson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: After, we will hear from Janet Jackson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And last, we will hear from Francisco Insframe.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And we've been joined by Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I did fail to recognize that Councilmember Brewer was in the room early.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hutchinson, formerly in shelter seven years, says security staff escalate conflict and ignored a resident who later died. He also describes being forced outside in winter while sick with shingles.
chapters.title: Denton Hutchinson describes neglect and mistreatment in shelters

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Denton Hutchinson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: My name is Denton Hutchinson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I'm with the Community Leadership Collective of the Coalition for the Homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I want to thank you for holding this long-awaited hearing today on safety in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I was in shelter for over seven years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: And only recently was able to get housing and leave shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: During my seven years in shelter, I was transferred around to many sites, but I saw the same issues at different shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: One of the hardest parts of living in a shelter is how people are treated by staff,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: including the security staff who were supposed to create a safe environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Whether it was DHS police or private security guards, they treated us with absolute disrespect and complete disregard for our lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Security guards don't de-escalate conflict, they only escalate them, or they just ignore it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: In one shelter I was in, I noticed someone sleeping on the floor in the back of the recreation room in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I pointed him out to the DHS shelter security staff stationed about six steps away from the recreation room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: They said that he had missed his bed check, so he had to sleep on the floor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Hours later in the afternoon, I came back and he was still lying there unmoving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I spoke with security staff again, DHS that is, telling them that he had moved since I saw him that morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: DHS security finally walked over to see him and discovered he was dead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: It was horrifying, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: He was someone that I knew, interacted with him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: They let him lay there, steps away all night and day without even bothering to check on him or do anything that could have saved his life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: This shows the security staff do not care about the lives of people in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: In other instances, I was sick with the worst case of shingles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Because of the shingles, I could only wear the lightest of clothing because it hurt so excruciatingly bad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: It was the middle of winter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: There was an altercation and the DHS police required all residents to leave the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I asked DHS staff if I could stay inside or go to my bed or another room because I was sick and didn't have winter clothes on and it was very cold out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: They said I had to leave and I stood outside in the cold wearing next to nothing, worried about apothema and my health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Again, this only goes to show that shelters and security staff do not care about the lives and well-being of shelter residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: Those of us who have no place to go but shelter deserves basic respect and dignity, but that is not what we get in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: I want to thank you for this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for sharing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Denton Hutchinson
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Jackson, formerly homeless five years, describes mice in mattresses, flooding, invasive staff entries, long commutes, and unaddressed grievances. She says safety means dignity and clean, maintained space.
chapters.title: Janet Jackson testifies on unsafe and unsanitary shelter conditions

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Janet Jackson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: My name is Janet Jackson with the Community Leadership Coalition, Leadership Collective at the Coalition for the Homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I am formerly homeless, but I

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I continue to fight the issues I faced while I was in the shelter for about five years, continue to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: One of the hardest parts about being in the shelter was the constant feeling of insecurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I stayed in a few different shelters, and some of them were in isolated parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: When I first entered the shelter, I was placed in a congregated shelter after intake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: There were mice nesting in the mattresses along with other insects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: The dorm rooms I lived in would flood during heavy rains.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Others could not put their belongings in the closet at the bottom because it would be ruined by the flooding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: During COVID, I was placed in a hotel because of my health issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Being in my own space made a huge difference, but even though I had my own room, staff was destructive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I would try to get some sleep after working a long shift at the hospital, but staff would come around, open the doors to every room without knocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: It didn't matter if you were undressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Some of these staff were male.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: They just opened the door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: It was very invasive and unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: When COVID emergency ended and they wanted to transfer me out of the hotel, I requested a shelter that was closer to my job and told them I needed a shelter that didn't require steps because I required a cane to walk and steps were hard for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: They told me the only shelter they could put me in was in East New York, Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: And this was a senior women's shelter, which was one and a half to two hours away from my job in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: at Jacoby Medical Center, where I worked the evening and the night shift.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I would often get back to the shelter for my shift at 1 to 2 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: In the morning after traveling on the train for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: And then when I get off the train, the L train, I felt unsafe because it was desolated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: And this is 1, 2 o'clock in the morning, and walking to the shelter, I felt unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: We made complaints to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: It's hard to get the staff to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I was having trouble breathing, and the day shift supervisor was making his rounds, and when he came to my room, I told him,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: that I was having difficulty because there must have been a mouse or something on the trap under the dresser.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: He told me it had to wait until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: When the next shift supervisor came at 4, I told her what happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: She seen I was having trouble breathing with my air conditioner on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Checked up underneath the dresser and there was two mice trapped in the trap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: The mice exhumated my asthma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: A shelter should be a place where people can find stability, but instead it's hard to get anything done or your basic needs met.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Safety means being treated with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: It means being able to sleep peacefully, having a clean and well-maintained place to stay, knowing that staff take shelter residents'concerns seriously,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: trusting that you will not be punished for speaking up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the council for inviting me here today and for this hearing to shine a light on all the problems in the shelter that still exists that make people feel unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Insfran, speaking in Spanish and English, says shelter staff are not trained to de-escalate, ignored his requests for a room key, and retaliated when he closed his door. He asks for basic respect and safety.
chapters.title: Francisco Insfran testifies on staff hostility and lack of safety

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And now we'll hear from Francisco Insfrain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Mi nombre es Francisco Insfran y soy miembro del colectivo de liderazgo comunitario de Coalición por Homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Gracias por la oportunidad que nos dan en esta audiencia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Esperaba encontrar estabilidad mientras trabajaba para conseguir una vivienda permanente.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Es difícil lograr esa estabilidad cuando no me siento seguro en el albergue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: My name is Francisco Insfran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Community Collective Coalition for Homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thanks to all of you here in the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm addressing to you because I don't feel safe in these homeless shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I was hoping to find stability while I was working to find a permanent home for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But it's very difficult to find stability when I don't find myself safe in one of these homeless places.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Uno de los aspectos más difíciles de vivir en un albergue es la forma en que tratan a los empleados de dieches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Se supone que ellos deben crear un entorno seguro para nosotros, sin embargo, cada vez que hay un conflicto entre ellos se crea un ambiente peligroso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.text: And instead, to give him the juice was a very big fight between both of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: Solo miraban o hacían que no entendían absolutamente nada.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: El destrozo fue grande.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Any of the people who were working at the shelter did anything to try to help in the situation or to stack the fire, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The only thing they were doing, they were looking at them at the same time they were fighting without doing anything, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And the fire was so bad that it even destroyed some of the kitchen utensils and some of the kitchen equipment that was there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And why we should have this cruel reaction from these people from the homeless shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Vas a ir de las, la tercera página.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: ¿Lo pueden ver?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Las con el que.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: ¿Puedes, verdad?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Sí.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Ok, tranquilo.

utterances.text: Los personal no están entrenados.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran
utterances.text: O sea, el personal, disculpa, de staff, no está entrenada realmente para crear un ambiente tranquilo y que pueda ser seguro para los residentes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francisco Insfran

chapters.summary: Erin Dalton, DSS Commissioner, thanks the panel and says procedures and data matter, but resident perceptions of safety and dignity are the most important measures she wants to track.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton acknowledges resident testimony and safety perceptions

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Erin Dalton, Commissioner for the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Before I begin with my testimony, I want to thank you for convening the panel of folks who came to testify about their experiences in our system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I do think it's really important to start with the voices of people.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And while you'll hear us testify, I'm about to testify to a lot of procedures, protocols, data that we think and we set up to keep people safe and to have their voices heard.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: None of it can address people's perceptions of those conditions if we don't hear from them directly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so while I, during my time here, will do my best work to make sure all those procedures, protocols are in place and that we use that data to help improve the system every single day,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: the most important measure to me will be people's perceptions of their safety, their sense of dignity, respect.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and how we treat them in the system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And those are measures we don't have in place at this time, but measures I can put in place and will put in place so that we can keep a pulse on what's really happening for the people who are serving in the system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So appreciate everyone's testimony and informing us on the issues they continue to see inside our system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Dalton says DHS oversees 502 shelters, seven city-run, with round-the-clock security, access controls, cameras, risk assessments, peace officers, and provider training on de-escalation and trauma-informed care.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton outlines DHS shelter security operations

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So moving on to more formal testimony, good afternoon, Chair Hudson and members of the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I am Erin Dalton, Commissioner for the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Joining me are Department of Homeless Services First Deputy Commissioner Christine Fellini and Deputy Commissioner for Shelter Service Security, LaVanche Priester.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss shelter safety and the legislation on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS oversees 502 shelter sites across New York City, seven of them operated directly by DHS.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are committed to protecting our clients, the staff who serve them, and the surrounding communities.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That means secure facilities, well-maintained buildings, and responding concerns promptly and transparently.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On the issues of security and safety.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our approach to safety includes on-site security, access controls, surveillance, staff training, incident reporting, and ongoing oversight.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every shelter has security around the clock.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Officers at each entrance control access and monitor cameras placed throughout the interior and exterior of the building.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Each facility's security needs depend on its location,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: layout, access points, and history.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS conducts security risk assessments to set staffing levels and equipment, which can include access control systems, cameras, metal detectors, and x-ray machines.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our goal is risk-based security that protects residents and staff while respecting their dignity.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS's 352 peace officers are deployed at intake and assessment sites and at facilities on Ward's Island, where they control access, maintain order, and respond to incidents.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The DHS Provider Assistance Unit trains security staff at provider-operated shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Training covers the foundations of the work, including understanding homelessness, cultural sensitivity, serving people with disabilities, and trauma-informed care, as well as practical skills such as de-escalation, crisis intervention, conflict

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: resolution, and suicide prevention.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: PAU and other uniformed staff can also assist providers during emergencies and support inspections to remove weapons, drugs, and other contraband.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When serious incidents occur, DHS responds and contacts emergency services when needed.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our serious incident unit operates around the clock, tracks more than 70 types of incidents, and reviews reports for accuracy, allowing us to spot trends and risks.

chapters.summary: Dalton explains good neighbor policies, community advisory boards, and safety transfers. She reports 2,654 safety transfers in FY26, slightly up from 2,625 in FY25.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton describes good neighbor policy and safety transfers

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Moving on to our good neighbor policy.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our neighbors are valuable partners through our nonprofit partnerships, volunteering, donations, and workforce programs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every shelter has a good neighbor policy that sets clear expectations for conduct inside the shelter and in the surrounding community.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents receive written rules when they are

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: arrive, providers reinforce those rules through case management and security monitors activity in and around the building.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Community advisory boards bring together providers, DHS, elected officials, community boards, local businesses, and neighbors, usually every quarter, giving the community a regular place to raise concerns.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The NYPD's Quality of Life Division reports on incidents at these meetings, and many providers attend monthly precinct council meetings.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When problems arise, responses range from conversations with staff to additional support, and when safety is at stake, a transfer.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: About client safety transfers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents may face threats, harassment, or violence that make their placement unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When a concern is raised, we may take immediate protective steps, contact law enforcement, or other emergency responders, or arrange a transfer depending on the urgency of the concern, the resident's needs, and the available placements.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There were 2,654 safety transfers in fiscal year 26, slightly up from the

chapters.summary: Dalton says 58% of shelter buildings predate 1980, DHS inspects and repairs, publishes a repair scorecard, and standard shelters average fewer than four open violations while flexible hotels average about 42.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton details shelter conditions and repair processes

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When it comes to shelter conditions, maintaining safety also depends on the conditions of our more than 500 buildings, which vary in age, size, ownership, and original purpose.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 58% of our buildings were built before 1980, and many were converted to shelter use to meet that demand.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Keeping them in good condition requires regular inspections, timely repairs, preventive maintenance, and long-term capital planning.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are closing older and substandard facilities and prioritizing purpose-built shelters designed around

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: trauma-informed care.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS regularly reviews provider performance on safety and building maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Routine site review inspections conducted with the provider staff and the Department of Buildings, Department of Housing Preservation and Development, the Fire Department, and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene identify code violations, hazards, and hazards before they become more serious.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Providers are expected to address severe deficiencies within 24 hours of receiving the results.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS publishes a quarterly shelter repair scorecard so New Yorkers can see the conditions in our shelter buildings.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Conditions in our standard shelters have improved dramatically since 2016 when the city's shelter repair squad cut open violations in traditional shelters by 83% in nine months.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Today, our 365 standard shelters average fewer than four open violations each, and only one in 10 is high priority.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Those numbers have held steady even as the system has grown, and city agencies have completed more than 4,300 inspections so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The challenge is in our flexible capacity system, which is about 169 sites, mostly commercial hotels, open to meet a surge in demand.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: These buildings average about 42 open violations each.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This is something to better understand and correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's also one reason we are reducing our reliance on hotels, particularly for families with children.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents and staff can also report problems through our shelter repair hotline.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Last year, the hotline received 2,934 complaints.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Each complaint is followed up by the resident and the provider, and for serious problems, Department of Buildings or HPD may inspect and issue violations.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Each repair has to be assessed as routine maintenance, an urgent fix, or a larger capital project.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS's Asset Information Management System documents capital needs in city-owned buildings, such as boilers, plumbing, electrical systems, fire alarms, roofs, elevators, and bathrooms.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There are 55 city and state-owned buildings in our portfolio, and major repairs must go through the city's capital program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For FY27, we have $106 million for 102 projects across 38 shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Eight are complete, and 31 are in active construction and expected to finish by June 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The rest are in planning, design, or procurement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For privately owned buildings, responsibility for repair depends on the provider's arrangement with the owner.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Providers responsible for routine maintenance have a budget for it, which varies with the site's age and layout.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When a larger repair is the provider's responsibility, our facilities and logistics team helps to identify solutions.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If the provider's budget can't cover the costs, we submit a request to OMB.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are reviewing these processes to remove administrative bottlenecks, give providers more visibility, and speed up repairs whenever possible.

chapters.summary: Dalton separates crime data from health and safety needs. She says arrests and serious violence are down, deaths fell from 512 to 305, but complaints about staff-client interactions rose 46%.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton presents crime and safety data trends

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Looking at what the data that we have shows as it pertains to shelter safety, I want to separate two different kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The first

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: is crime information.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Those are NYPD complaints and arrests at our shelter addresses, serious violent incidents tracked in the mayor's management report, and complaints residents make to DSS about assault, harassment, and how they are treated.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The second is day-to-day health and safety needs of the people we serve, which show up in 911 calls and incidents our providers report.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: A medical emergency is not a crime, so these need to be counted and considered separately.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'll share rates per thousand so that the great growth in the shelter population doesn't distort the trends.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Looking at part one, crime and safety complaints.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Arrests at shelter addresses have fallen per resident since FY23, and serious violence is declining.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The mayor's management report shows that in single adult shelters where the rates are the highest, serious violent incidents fell 13% last year to 2.8 per 1,000 residents, down from 4.8 in FY22.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In family shelters, the rate fell or held steady at well below 1 per 1,000.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents'own complaints add something police data can't compare.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: can't capture, rather.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Complaints to DSS about discrimination, assault, and harassment rose 19% this year, and complaints about interactions between staff and clients rose 46%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: More people are raising complaints, not just the same people calling more often.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: These complaints tell us residents don't always feel safe or respected, and that's something we can take direct action to improve.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Looking at the health and safety needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Calls include calls made by staff, and close to 40% of those are medical.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So many reflect people getting the help when they need it.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Calls per resident rose last year, most sharply in safe havens and stabilization sites, which serve people with some of the most significant needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are watching calls about disputes and disorders most closely because they are also rising.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Calls about assault and violence are a small share, and they have fallen since fiscal year 23.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Incidents reported by providers have been roughly level.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: A third are accidents, health concerns, and hospitalizations.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Serious incidents among single adults have declined each year since fiscal year 23.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Including a 13% drop over the last two years.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The most serious measure of safety is found in the mortality data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The death rate in shelter has fallen by two-thirds in three years, from about 11 per thousand residents in FY22 to 3.5 in FY25, the lowest since fiscal year 2018.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Part of that reflects a younger population with more children, but the number of deaths also fell from 512 to 305, while the shelter population nearly doubled.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Drug-related deaths across the homeless population fell 28% last year, but still account for 40% of all deaths, and 42 of the 73 people who died in a shelter in FY25 died of an overdose.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The people we serve are also getting older.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The share of deaths amongst people 65 and older rose from 13% to 17% in one year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Naloxone in every building, treatment and medical care for an aging population are safety measures as well.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The overall picture is real progress with clear work ahead.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Arrests and serious violence are down and fewer people are dying in our care.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: At the same time, conflicts, condition in our commercial hotels and residents'concerns about how they are treated show us that there's where our focus needs to be.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our goal is shelters that are safe and dignified for everyone who lives and works in them.

chapters.summary: Dalton supports transparency but says DHS cannot publish disaggregated security information and already reports to state bodies. On Intro 99, she says DHS tries to place families near the youngest child's school but zip code data may miss DV circumstances.
chapters.title: Commissioner Dalton comments on Intro 387 and Intro 99

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 0387, I'm going to move on to that now and comment on the two introductions for today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That introduction would require DHS to produce an annual report on critical incidents in our shelters, along with information on security measures, security upgrades, and agreements with NYPD and other law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We do share the goal of transparency.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS already reports critical incidents to state oversight bodies, including OTDA, OCFS, and through the Mayor's Management Report.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We would seek to align any new requirements with these existing systems to avoid duplicate reporting.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We also must protect confidential shelter information.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS cannot publish some security information disaggregated by individual shelter as the introduction requires.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Public reporting would need to aggregate data and protect confidential addresses.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the sponsor and council on legislation that advances transparency while meeting these privacy obligations.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 0099 would require DHS to report annually on the number and share of families with children.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Placed in shelter in the same or an adjoining zip code as their last address.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We welcome further conversation with the sponsor on the goals of this bill.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS makes every effort to place families near the youngest child's school, and the mayor's management report already checks the share of families placed in the borough of that school.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Zip code data may not capture the factors behind placement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For example, families affected by domestic violence may need to be placed away from their prior address.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We welcome discussion of reporting that accounts for these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In conclusion, I appreciate the Council's attention to ensuring that shelters are safe, secure, and well-maintained.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We welcome your questions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.text: Kick it off with a few questions and then I'm going to turn to my colleagues in just a moment's time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What has led to the increase?

utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I mean, I think obviously we are a right-to-shelter city and proud to be one, and the increase in need from the asylum population certainly overwhelmed the system that DHS was operating during that time.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I'm personally grateful for all of the work that the city and the Department of Homeless Services did to open so many shelters in such a short period in order to accommodate that need.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton

utterances.text: Christine Fellini, First Deputy Commissioner at the Department of Homeless Services.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Not as we've decided to move towards more

utterances.text: You went through, obviously, deaths and incidents in the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I'm wondering, you called out specifically the older adult population as well as those with substance use disorder.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I'm wondering...

utterances.text: I don't have those numbers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think we are seeing an increase in the share of older adults using our shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I'm not certain that we track precisely the number of people who have a diagnosis or are experiencing substance use disorder, but we could certainly see what we have and get back to the council.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It would be interesting to know, you know, whether it's at intake or obviously people who are being sent to specific or sent to shelters who provide specific services, you know, what those numbers look like and how they've changed.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: over time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, one second.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, and then one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You mentioned that the death rate in shelter has fallen by two-thirds in three years, from about 11 per 1,000 residents in fiscal year 2022

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And that part of that reflects a younger population with more children, while also a greater population of older adults.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So if you can just provide a little bit more clarity on those numbers.

utterances.text: I was also just trying to put into context the very significant decline in mortality data is also a function of who we're serving in the system.

utterances.text: But we can obviously provide the changing demographics of the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions specifically pertaining to...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: your testimony, I'd like to turn it over to my colleagues and then I'll get into my long list of questions.

chapters.summary: Morano asks when DHS will provide legal analysis on declining a VA grant for homeless veterans. He then asks whether community advisory boards only function after shelter siting decisions are made.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions Dalton on VA grant and advisory boards

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So starting with Councilmember Murano, followed by Wilson, and then Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before I ask you a little bit about your testimony today, you were kind enough to testify before the last committee hearing that

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Hudson and I co-chaired, and you indicated that you'd get us some information about the legal analysis that the city relied upon to decline the VA grant for homeless veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you have any idea when you might be able to get that to us?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't, as I said here, but we can respond in writing with a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In your testimony, you discussed the good neighbor policy and community advisory boards.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And you say these boards bring together elected officials, community boards, businesses, and neighbors to discuss concerns.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But isn't it true that these advisory boards generally function?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: After the city has already decided where to put a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So the neighborhood gets a chance to discuss problems after the decision's already been made, but not necessarily a meaningful opportunity to raise concerns before the decision's finalized.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is that a fair characterization?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think it's fair that the community advisory boards are set up to be a good neighbor with the shelter that is there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think it's right to characterize it as an ongoing process with the community.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But certainly we work with community boards and electeds and community members.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Aligned with the process that we use to site shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So there is engagement with community prior to...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Wouldn't it make more sense to conduct a community impact assessment and solicit neighborhood input before committing taxpayer dollars to a location rather than asking residents to live with the consequences and complain afterward?

utterances.text: I appreciate that as a sentiment, and we can certainly take back as we look at any potential changes to the way we do shelter siting in the city.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano notes 2,654 safety transfers and asks who is moved when a resident is threatened. Fellini says it depends; if the victim wants to stay, the alleged perpetrator may be transferred. Safety transfer is the disciplinary consequence.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions safety transfers and perpetrator discipline

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One other question before I run out of time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You report that DHS conducted 2,654 safety transfers last fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's more than seven people being transferred every single day because of safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When a resident is threatened or assaulted by another resident,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Who gets moved, the victim or the person responsible for the threat?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to let my colleagues answer here, and then I'm also going to think through the math of that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Because people move in and out of the shelter system, so I don't think the denominator is right.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It wouldn't be the first time I made a math error.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But the substance of the question is important, so I'm going to ask my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It depends on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If the person who is the victim of the assault prefers to stay at the shelter, it is possible that we will transfer the alleged perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there any disciplinary consequence for an individual who repeatedly threatens or assaults other shelter residents?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The safety transfer is the way we do that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we're looking to maintain the safety of people in the shelter as well as the staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We're also looking to get at what the issue is that is causing the individual to act out in this way.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So that's also making sure they're in the shelter that either provides the right services or connect them to community services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I may have more questions for you later.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

chapters.summary: Wilson asks about de-escalation and sensitivity training. Fellini says DHS trains over 15,000 staff through the HEARTS curriculum and follows up on complaints to see if training is implemented.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson questions DHS on de-escalation and trauma training

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Moving on to Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hello, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: From the testimony we heard in the first panel, there were many instances about conflicts that they're having with staff in the shelters.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So does DSS...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Have rules around de-escalation and sensitivity training for providers, staff, and how is that, how do you conduct oversight to ensure that those are happening?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, and I mean, while my colleagues look up the actual numbers, perhaps, I mean, yes, we do have training and support for those very kinds of efforts.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think I testified, too, that we saw increases in those kinds of complaints.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So we're seeing it not just in hearing it, not just from the people who testified today, but seeing it across the board.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And it may be an area where we need to do more, but I will let my colleagues speak to the specifics there.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, and thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And I think you're hitting on a good point.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We can train.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We have to make sure that the training is in.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So related to trauma-informed training as per local law 49 of 2023, we've trained in the last two years over 15,000 staff around customer service with a focus on what we call HEARTS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And this is really

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: to make sure that we have a holistic trauma-informed approach to the work that we do.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: This is every level of staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: This is every day of the week.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we really want to make sure that everyone is implementing the training.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And while they may be contracted provider staff at the shelter, it's DHS's responsibility to make sure that that ethos is permeated throughout the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are the trainings, is it up to the provider to do the trainings or implement the trainings, or does DSS do those?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: DHS offers the training and requires staff to take it.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We then follow up, and I think it's part of the review of complaints and incidents to the point the commissioner made about what we're seeing the increase in.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That says something to us.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we say, listen, we implemented HARTS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: What's going on at your facility?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is it staff-related?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is it facility-related?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is it related to a particular client or clients?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So it allows us to dig into what's going on at a particular site.

utterances.text: And to the Commissioner's point earlier, we have procedures and we have protocols, and the grievance process is one of them.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's a longstanding procedure, and as I believe Mr.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Denton, I hope I got his name right,

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Testified, right?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I give the form to the person I might be having an issue with.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So that is the policy.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Clients do have the opportunity to essentially appeal the shelter's response to that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we do track those and may get involved.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Community members, clients, anyone can also report complaints or inquiries to us at DSS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: through 311.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They can come into one of our centers and make a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They can call us and make a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And all of that is gathered and analyzed.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we're looking not just at individual complaints, we're looking at trends.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is there a particular shelter?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is someone named repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Because then we're going to dig in.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We expect the shelter already has, but as program staff, we're also going to get the shelter director on the phone to say what's going on with this person.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And how can we help?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Because that's the other thing.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how follow-up works. Fellini says the ombudsman contacts about 90% of complainants, shelters have three to five days to respond, and DHS monitors for patterns or need for transfer.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson asks how complainants learn their grievance was addressed

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Well, then how is the follow-up with the person making the report?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How do they know that their complaint has been taken seriously and that DSS is going to take all these steps to analyze their complaint?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Part of the process that is implemented by the ombudsman's office at DSS is, one, to let the complainant know that we've received the inquiry and directed it to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So that's step one.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They have a pretty good success rate of 90%, contacting about 90% of the people who have complained.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are some instances where somebody's voicemail isn't set up or we can't get in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's then passed on to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They have three to five days to respond.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: DSS is also made aware, sorry, DHS is made aware of the complaint.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We're CC'd on everything that goes out to the shelters that we're responsible for.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And then we monitor.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If this is related to one particular staff, we want to know what the next steps are.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is this training?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Is this not the right shelter?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Could this person be transferred to a different shelter in the provider's portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Or do we need additional action?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But we're actively involved in making sure that the complaints get addressed and that if it's a one-time thing, if we're seeing this over time, that it's not just addressing the complaints, it's us taking a deep dive into what's happening at that shelter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If I may add, I mean, I think some of this is actually the way, the process by which we must collect complaints are state reg.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so there are just some rules around the way we're required to do that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But it is also why I think, you know, building out the direct communication with residents of the shelter system so we can hear on an ongoing basis as an additional tool to understand and support

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: their well-being, I feel like is a critical piece to be built.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It just would be useful to understand if you think it would add value in understanding that or if this specific measure, which speaks to the youngest child and keeping them in their district.

utterances.text: If you can, you can't always do it.
