chapters.summary: Ung asks how non-English speakers navigate grievances. Fellini says shelters must comply with language access policy and have a 24-hour language line; DHS does not track provider staff language capabilities but encourages diverse staff.
chapters.title: Council Member Ung questions DHS on language access in grievances

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: To Councilmember Ong, followed by Councilmember Nurse, and then Councilmember Aviles.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And we've been joined by Councilmember Aviles.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Commissioner, for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So I do have a question about the language capabilities of shelters.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: If your client where English is not their first language, how do they go through the grievance procedure, either written or oral?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And then how does the message get communicated back to the client?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: All shelters are required to comply with the language access policy and all have access to DHS's language line contract to be able to communicate with every single client 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If it were the grievance process, just like with any form, staff would use the language line to make sure the client understood the form, talk through that, help record the response.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The form would live.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: In English back to the shelter staff or to DHS, and the language line could assist with making sure that the client understood what the process is.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, is there any, and I appreciate the language line, always do appreciate the language line, but is there any effort

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: you know, depending on where the shelter is, the community that is in the shelter system, the language they speak, is there any effort to, you know, hire people in the shelter that speaks that language?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we want our providers to make sure that there's a diverse shelter staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So, yes.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Is there, okay, I mean, is there any statistics on this, any examples of this that can be helpful and, like, for me to understand a little bit more of what is going on?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah, we don't track the language capability of provider staff, but it's something we could certainly look into.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And there is an effort to communicate to providers that, you know, that it should be the language, hopefully the language that, you know, that, you know, that's, that actually is spoken in that shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we have communi cards, which make it easy for clients to indicate to staff what language they speak so that saves some time and not back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Aviles says case management and CityFEPs support is inadequate. Fellini says the housing specialist ratio is about 1 to 40 at sites that have them, but some sites lack housing specialists.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles questions DHS on housing specialist ratios

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilman Raviles?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So we've heard from a number of our constituents living in shelters that case management services, particularly getting support with securing housing via city FEPS vouchers, is really inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So one of our constituents came to our office crying because she has lost out on two apartments when she wasn't able to get support from her housing specialist.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: What's the current ratio of the housing specialist to shelter residents?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And given that our goal with the shelter system is to get, hopefully, people out of shelters and into permanent dignified housing, what's the ideal ratio that we should have of housing specialists to residents?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Our shelters are budgeted along a OMB-approved model budget.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So those model budgets set the ratios of staff that are budgeted for, with some exceptions if the provider wants to rearrange some of the lines or the titles.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Currently, for sites that do have housing specialists,

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The ratio is about 1 to 40.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are some sites that do not have housing specialists.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I would say, title aside, it's imperative that any case management staff be able to advocate on behalf of the client.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So they need to know the vouchering process.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They need to know all the options for a household.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They need to make sure the household is aware of what they might qualify for, what they do qualify for, and then take steps to help them get that voucher or housing strategy and then assist with finding housing.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: As it relates to the CityFEP's process, I know our colleagues at HRA have done a lot to improve the processing time, and I know we continue to look at that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we get a lot of inquiries from shelter staff about why is it taking so long.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So, again, we're looking at the system on our side, the processing, when somebody does find housing.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But we look to support our shelter providers to make sure that the staff on the ground supporting clients are doing so effectively.

chapters.summary: Aviles asks how many housing specialists citywide and how performance is tracked. Fellini says she does not have the number and DHS measures success by CityFEPs placements.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles asks about citywide housing specialist numbers and performance

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: If I could ask a quick follow-up, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In terms of, you mentioned OMB is setting the ratios.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of what is determining, what criteria is OMB using to determine whether or not

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: our housing crisis is critical enough to actually make sure we have housing specialists that can make sure we get people out of the shelter system?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah, and let me clarify, OMB doesn't set the...

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: ratio.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's a model that we have

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: negotiated with OMB.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So there are, you know, depending on the capacity of the site, a certain number of staff to meet the critical core functions of what should happen in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So do you know how many housing specialists do you have citywide?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And do you track performance around those housing specialists?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke

utterances.text: That's certainly something we could follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And our measure of success, again, not related to that role specifically, but is CityFEP's placements and all placements to be.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We know assistance comes in many forms, and permanent housing could come through a voucher or through many other means.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: We'd love to hear more about how DHS is securing staffing capacity to help make sure that residents are transitioning out of the shelter system, and how do we ensure that that is a robust and supportive environment.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DHS ensures DV survivors are sent to safe housing. Fellini describes DV screening, NOVA referrals, separating the alleged abuser, and following exclusion recommendations.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on DV survivor shelter safety

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: When DV survivors seek shelter, how does DHS ensure that they're sent to a safe housing situation?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: First and foremost, when somebody comes into DHS, we are doing a domestic violence screening.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So somebody doesn't have to necessarily state that, but through our assessment process, we may be referring the person who comes in or the family to HRA's NOVA, No Violence Again program.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And they're really assessing criteria and eligibility for placement into a domestic violence shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And what they're doing is making sure that if there is a parent DV and they cannot take this household in due to capacity constraints or the size of the family doesn't meet the available units in a DV

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: shelter, that they're making DHS placements aware.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And what happens there is if there is a parent DV, we are going to separate the alleged abuser from the alleged victim if the household is coming together.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We will refer the alleged abuser to the single adult side while we place the remaining household.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If this is an instance of DV and there is a parent DV, but it's not within household members, we're making sure that we follow NOVA's recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: for areas of exclusion, and those tend to be specific addresses or zip codes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.text: We have diversion and mediation

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: policies, and that really helps to standardize the approach.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But again, each engagement with each individual household is going to be different depending on their circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But in terms of diversion and mediation, the goal is to avoid shelter, right?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Somebody came to us and said, I have a housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think I need shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Our goal is to see how, if at all, we can reconnect you to community resources.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So at our resource room, we have social workers that can complete mediation with a primary tenant or a different housing option.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And that might be as simple as calling up the primary tenant to say, hey, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Christine was living with you and things weren't okay.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Can we make this work?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: What could help resolve this situation?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So that's the mediation process that happens at Path at Resource Room.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And again, we're also making sure that that option is safe.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We ask very pointed questions about DV in the house.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: In the housing option that we're on the phone with or communicating with, we don't want to send families into an unsafe situation.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We're also looking to make sure that there's sufficient space in that housing option.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So those are the ways we make sure that we're diverting to safe options.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about reducing density. Dalton says DHS is on track to comply with Executive Order 2 limiting single adult capacity to 200 beds by 2027 and purpose-built shelters average about 160 beds.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on reducing shelter density

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Large congregate shelters create an environment where there is likely to be more interpersonal conflict.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What steps is DHS taking to reduce density in shelter sites?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: First, we are on track to comply with Mayor Ron Donnie's Executive Order 2, which requires that single adults'capacity remain at 200 beds or less by the end of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So we're pleased about that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And our purpose-built shelters, which I think are certainly the way we're trying to move the system, there's 32 of those.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 25 have been open in the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: They all have smaller dorms, and they're smaller capacity in general.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the average over those sites is about 160.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And importantly, it's not just the overall size of the building and the number of people there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It is also the density of the dorm space so that people are more comfortable where they're staying.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DHS decides to repair or close shelters like Bellevue. Fellini says closure is a last resort, based on enforcement agency advice and engineering reports; DHS prefers remediation.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on Bellevue closure and repair decisions

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And we often hear about the poor condition of shelter facilities.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The Bellevue men's shelter was closed in April 2026 due to severe disrepair and unsafe building conditions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How does DSS decide which shelters to repair or in the case of Bellevue, which to close entirely?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In reference to Bellevue, I'll answer this question as the Commissioner pointed out.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There are really two approaches to this.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: One is for publicly owned, city or state owned facilities, and the other are privately owned.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So when it comes to publicly owned shelters, obviously,

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The last resort is to close a facility, and we would only do that on the advice of our enforcement agencies like Department of Buildings or FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And this requires architect and engineering reports.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's a very big decision to make.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But what we...

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Do day to day is maintain our buildings, right?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we have a long-term interest in keeping our buildings.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And the way we're assessing is how much money are we spending on repairs over time?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: What are the results of a building inspection?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: What notifications, complaints, incidents are happening at particular shelters?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And again, the goal is not to close, but it's to remediate.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And again, that's really how for the capital side, the publicly owned buildings, we try to maintain and repair rather than close.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how many shelters need significant repairs. Fellini says DHS tracks 55 publicly owned buildings but does not readily track private buildings; 268 new needs are pending for 95 shelters.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on capital projects and repair timelines

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then I know, Commissioner, you referenced the capital program and specific projects as well as funding.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm wondering if there are shelters that need significant repairs and how many and how long will the repairs take?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: As the Commissioner mentioned, we do have quite a few capital projects for our 55 publicly owned buildings.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: When it comes to privately owned buildings, that is not something that we readily track.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we can't answer for the remainder of the over 500 buildings in the DHS portfolio how many need significant repairs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So there's no process that exists where you all are aware of significant capital needs in privately owned shelters?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are processes.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And one thing we can point to, it's not a perfect...

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Answer to the question, but one proxy, is our new needs process.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So as the Commissioner mentioned, when a privately owned building needs significant repairs that cannot be funded through their budget, we understand what the scope is and we make a request to OMB.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That's the new needs process.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We currently have 268 new needs pending in various statuses for 95 shelters.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That will include things that are likely not serious, but it does give us some sense of the scope.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So that's just broad new needs, not...

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Facility-related new needs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But that could be...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Doors to shower stalls or something like that as opposed to roof repairs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: There's no way to parse out.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we'd have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Our data system, we're working on some enhancements to better allow us to analyze the data rather than having to read every single request.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But routine repairs like replacing a shower door normally come out of the provider's budget.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Every provider, if they have maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So it wouldn't be considered a new need in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Just again, as a proxy for Sirius.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: New need is a proxy for serious, you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But serious as determined by the owner of the building, the private operator?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: No, the provider and DHS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Oh, and DHS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So the provider, this is coming from our contracted providers that say, listen, I'm maxed out in my maintenance line or my maintenance budget does not allow for this major repair.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We agree, we look at the scope, we look at the bids, and we request the funding from OMB.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DHS chooses capital projects and design principles. Fellini says all 55 public buildings are eligible, ranked by need, and DHS relies on providers' visions for design.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on capital project selection and design

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is DHS's process for choosing capital projects to fund?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And again, all of the 55 publicly owned buildings are eligible for capital.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we're not choosing.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We are kind of

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: ranking where the need is and where the project is in terms of the multi-year process that unfortunately a capital project needs to go through.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are many steps involving different agencies.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So again, we identify through our, the Commissioner mentioned our AIMS system, our asset management system.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We're looking at violations.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We're looking at various formal and informal inspections, complaints, incidents to identify the priority repairs that are needed.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And those go to the top of the list of capital request projects.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And how does DHS work with providers on shelter repairs for city-owned facilities?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And that's the capital process.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So in addition, DHS operates only a handful of sites, even though we have 55 publicly owned.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The providers are contracted to operate most of those.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And what I just described is the same process, whether a provider is operating it or the city is.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what design and architectural principles does DHS use when designing shelters?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Does this differ for different shelter populations?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So thank you for the question, and it is an interesting one.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: DHS does not have design principles.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think what we rely on is the provider and their vision for what services they want to provide, the population they want to provide.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So when they bring a site to us or the plan for a site, they're already thinking, what population do I want to serve and how do I want to serve them?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we rely on them and their discussions with architects and developers to kind of propose.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: to us their ideal shelter.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So what about the purpose-built shelters?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You wouldn't...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites 3.82 violations per standard shelter and 37.56 per flexible shelter. Dalton says hotels are non-residential buildings and applying residential code inflates violations; Fellini says not every violation is an active hazard.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on high violation rates in flexible shelters

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The most recent shelter repair scorecard showed an average of 3.82 building violations per standard shelter and 37.56 violations per flexible capacity shelter.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And you mentioned, I think, earlier that the flexible shelter conditions are challenging.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Why is the number of violations in flexible shelters so high?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And is DSS taking action to correct the issue?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And as I read my testimony aloud, I was reflecting on what I've learned since preparing the testimony.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so it is a good opportunity to correct the record a little bit on that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I'm going to let the deputy commissioner go into more detail.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But it isn't–

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Clearly, there's a differentiation between the mostly commercial hotels and the level of violation and our purpose-built and other shelters that have very low.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But it is also a function of the way hotels were built and applying a residential code onto those non-residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I don't want to give anyone here the impression that it is actually that much worse.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's a technicality to that, nor that we can't fix it.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think the data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: in this case, require some nuance, and I'd love to pass it to the Deputy Commissioner to provide that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And I think distinguishing between flexible capacity or standard capacity, regardless of the type of capacity, it's DHS's responsibility to work with the provider to make sure that those locations are safe for all the clients we serve.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: To the Commissioner's point about the hotels having different types of code versus the HPD inspection, that is done for our shelters that follow a residential.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Code, the same does not apply at hotels.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we're applying a residential code to a hotel that doesn't follow the same code.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: However, we are still responsible for making sure that those issues are resolved and that the locations are safe.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Also on violations, as we dig in, not every violation is an active safety hazard.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The hazard could have been remediated, but there may still be an administrative function that the building owner has not submitted the required paperwork to HPD to close that out off the website.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That is something else that we track as well.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites Local Law 154 requiring reporting on air conditioners. Fellini says DHS is preparing the report due in a few days and is not ready to discuss.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about air conditioner availability in shelters

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all for the answers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm going to take a page out of your book.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You always thank us for the questions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm going to thank you for the answers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: As temperatures continue to rise, the ability to stay cool becomes more of a health issue.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Local Law 154 of 2025 requires DSS to report on the availability of air conditioners in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you speak about what you've found in terms of the feasibility of providing air conditioners in shelters and what percentage of shelters already have air conditioners?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We are preparing the report that is due in a few days, so we are not ready to discuss yet.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that answer.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites NYPD data showing arrests rose from 405 in Q3 FY25 to 512 in Q4. Dalton says she is integrating data, questions NYPD data quality, and notes arrest is a measure of police activity.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on increase in shelter arrests

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: According to NYPD's precinct-level homeless shelter arrest data, in Q4 of fiscal year 2025, there were a total of 512 arrests.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: There were 405 arrests in Q3.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: To what do you attribute the increase in arrests in Q4 of FY25?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: How about we stop thanking for the questions?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But just now it's a habit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the issue of trying to align and integrate the important data that comes from other reporting sources like the NYPD is something that is very important to me.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I've spent the last couple of weeks really trying to integrate the arrest data, the complaint data, the 911 data, along with our

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: incident reporting data, our complaint data, into one set of information that we can then use on a very regular basis to manage the system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will say we're close to having that data integrated and usable, but not quite there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so just like you, I'm relying on the data that's publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And this is from quarterly reporting.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: that NYPD was producing and actually stopped after 2025.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I believe it's actually no longer required.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I just want to assure you it is of utmost interest to me to be able to

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: observe and take action on areas where we're seeing improvements, and we can model those improvements in other places as well as places where we're seeing concerns.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I do actually have some

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: questions about the quality of the data that NYPD was reporting here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But for the quarters that you actually asked about, quarter three of 2025 and quarter four of 2025, we do see something similar in our data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So we do see an increase in reported incidents during that period.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so we may

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: these two things might be correct and observing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And again, I reported on some of those observations in the data that we have.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so while I don't have an explanation, it is something we should work with NYPD to look at.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will say arrest is probably not the best measure of incident.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It is more of a measure of police activity.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think in combination with those other set of measures can help us to understand a picture, but alone, I think, don't also tell us all that much about what's happening in our system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites Gothamist reporting on fights and Priority 1 incidents at Tillery. Fellini says incidents decreased 48% for P1s and 45% overall since BRC took over.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on Tillery Street shelter safety improvements

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I want to ask a few questions about

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The Tillery Street Women's Shelter, which is in my district.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Recent reporting from Gothamist brought public attention to that shelter where there were at least 260 fights and disputes in 2024, which was a 72% increase from 2019.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The report found that the number of Priority 1 serious incidents is more than twice the citywide average for single adult shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you believe that shelter safety conditions have changed since Bowery Residence Committee or BRC took over from the Institute for Community Living or ICL as the shelter operator earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Just numerically, the rate of incidents has decreased 48% since against calendar year 25 in P1s alone, 45% overall.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And I think what was...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, 41% overall?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: 45% overall, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Dalton provides Tillery data: 911 calls down 13% to 1,248 in FY26, assault/violence calls down 41% from peak, PD complaints down to 207, felony reports down to 21, and felony arrests down to 12.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson reviews Tillery 911, complaint, and arrest data with DHS

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And actually, if I can add in there, this one, we worked hard to make sure with the NYPD we're correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I do have 911 PD incident complaints to report as well as arrests there to add to what the deputy commissioner provided if you'd like those.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And as you know, 911 is not just crime, it's medical and so on.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So 911 calls are down 13% from FY25.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The numbers in 26 were 1,248.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And in FY25, they were 1,429.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So this is the lowest 911 set of calls since FY22.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Still staying with 911, assault and violence calls are down 41% from their peak in FY24.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: About a third of the calls are ambulance calls.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then if you'd like to hear the PD complaint reports, these are incidents.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We love data, so please.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Crime incident data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 207 in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's, again, the lowest since FY22.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The peak was 263 in FY24.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And felony reports fell from 36 in FY22 to 21 in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, the 207 in FY26 and 263 in FY24 were which types of calls?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Those were PD complaint calls.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think about them as incident reports.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think they call them PD complaints.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And felonies also dropped.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Dropped, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: RERAS dropped as well.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So 54 in FY26, that's the lowest in five years.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Felony arrests fell from 33 to 12.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what caused the drop. Fellini credits a new provider, reassessments, transfers, and repairs. Dalton and Fellini say they have not visited Tillery; Hudson invites them.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks why Tillery incidents dropped and whether DHS visited

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And to what do you attribute the drop in all of these numbers?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think a new agency brings the opportunity for a new perspective.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: All the clients there were reassessed, which would be a normal course of business when there's a change in provider.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think, you know, in doing that assessment, some clients whose needs were better met elsewhere were transferred.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are also some repairs that the provider is doing to the building to try to improve the facilities.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So I think we've seen some...

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: improvements with the provider change that have likely contributed to the reduction.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And would you say that those are site configuration and daily operations?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Changes to site configuration and daily operations?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Daily operations for sure.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The site configuration is harder.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The building is the building.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's a limited site.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So I'd have to look into what, if any, building changes were made.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, fair, and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And have you all visited that site and met with residents and the staff at BRC?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I have not, no.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Commissioner?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I have not either.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I welcome you to visit.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I have been there since BRC has been there.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what site-level metrics DHS tracks. DHS says incidents, complaints, and grievances. Dalton says integrated data could show Tillery improvements. DHS does not know current Tillery staffing.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about site-level safety metrics and Tillery staffing

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I have a few more questions about this specifically, and then I'm going to go into round two for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What site-level metrics does the agency track to understand shelter safety?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: At site level, we track incidents, we track complaints, we track grievances.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If I may add, I mean, I do think as we get this data in order, you could see with Tillery that we could provide a whole set of measures that are all going in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And that gives at least me confidence that there's important improvements happening there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Hopefully we can add additional measures to that, including, again, client experience and regular feedback from clients on their experience in the system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And do you know how many staff are on site at Tillery now compared to last year?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what DHS has done since June 2026 to refresh Tillery under a new operator. DHS says nothing to add.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson follows up on Tillery shelter long-term plans

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You kind of got to this, but I'm just going to state the question for the record, and then if you have anything to add, feel free.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And if not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But in the committee's June 2026 hearing, Commissioner Dalton, you said the Tillery Shelter presented an opportunity to shape longer-term plans for the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What has DSS done since to act on that opportunity and to refresh the site under the new operator?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson reads an email from a city employee alleging discrepancies in reporting and a security contractor retained despite a DHS recommendation not to renew. Fellini says DHS investigates impropriety and may refer to DOI.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on security contractor conflicts and oversight

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would like to share.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: an email that I received, and I'm going to do my best to redact lots of the information.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: There were some specifics that were provided in an attempt to protect this person's identity, but

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: they have, they are a New York City employee who has elevated several security concerns with a single shelter provider, including one matter that they believed warranted referral to DOI

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: after they identified discrepancies between what was reported to DHS and what they were able to observe through records.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And DHS security personnel had provided, had recommended that the provider not renew with the same security contractor due to ongoing concerns.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And though that recommendation was known to staff, the contractor was still retained.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so I'm wondering, broadly speaking, what type of oversight structure and safeguards exist to prevent conflicts of interest, preferential treatment, or inappropriate relationships

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: with contracted providers and city leadership?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And, you know, we've...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Been through

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: a lot of this in the last mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so just want to make sure we have some real transparency around processes that you all have in place to identify inappropriate, you know, instances like this.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: These are serious allegations.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So if I heard you correctly, there were discrepancies in the records and things reported to DHS as well as concerns about the security contractor.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That were raised to DHS.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: When we are made aware, either directly through an incident, through a complaint, through an anonymous source of any impropriety, we investigate.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we will do some due diligence within DHS before making sure that we get that right over to DSS Legal, to the Office of Regulatory Compliance, to our ACCO, to do the legal and contractual steps that they do.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Which may also result in a referral to DOI.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It's possible, I don't know with certainty, but it's possible that this may have already been referred to DOI, but I suppose you and I will both find out in due time.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah, and we certainly welcome working with DOI.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's a resource to us to take investigations to a further place.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I don't want to belabor the point, but is it worth an X?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: explanation of the ways in which our providers contract with subcontractors and our role in that?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's, now would be an appropriate time.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about provider subcontracts and termination. Fellini says providers manage subcontracts, DSS ACCO approves, and DHS can recommend termination. Dalton says DHS can terminate primary contracts, not subcontracts.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on subcontractor termination authority

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Specific to security or food vendors or maintenance contracts, our nonprofits have the ability to decide to contract that work out.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: They do their market research.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Get bids from interested vendors and go with the lowest bidder who's able to be responsive to the ask.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The provider is responsible for managing that contract.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: DSS ACCO approves the subcontract, but the provider is ultimately responsible for implementing and making sure that the contractor is meeting the requirements of the subcontract.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And do you all have the authority to terminate a contract at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Let's just to clarify, sorry, now I'm asking questions myself, but we have authority to terminate contracts with our primary contractor.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, contracts.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But not necessarily with the subcontractor.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm reading Christine's.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That relationship is between the provider and the subcontractor.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We can recommend.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You could recommend, and then if they are...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If they choose not to terminate based on your recommendation, when is the next, when would be the first opportunity for you all to then engage or is there no opportunity for you to engage at all with a subcontractor?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Because I would assume that once that subcontract reaches the end of its term,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: then perhaps you all could insert yourselves and say we don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We're checking.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Hudson announces a two-minute second round, starting with Morano, then Brewer, then Aviles.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson begins second round of questions

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: With that, I'll take a quick pause, brief pause.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm going to stick to the two minutes for my second round of questions here from colleagues, but starting with Councilmember Barano, followed by Brewer, and then Aviles.

chapters.summary: Morano asks if 42 open violations per hotel would be acceptable for a private landlord. Dalton says residential code applied to hotels inflates violations but DHS must improve. She says she is integrating data to measure surrounding community impact.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions DHS on hotel violations and community impact

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: For the record, I strongly prefer the five-minute clock to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And that's why it's my hearing, and I've got two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Duly noted, Jim.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I know your preference, council member.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Duly noted.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, you testified earlier.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You acknowledged that flexible capacity shelters, which are mostly commercial hotels,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Average, approximately five.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 42 open violations per facility, 42.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If a private landlord had 42 outstanding building violations, would the city consider that an acceptable place to house vulnerable New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's a good opportunity to provide clarification.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm not 100% sure if you were in the room just a few minutes ago when we went through this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: As I indicated, as I read my testimony aloud, I learned some things in this process of preparing the testimony about how hotels are different and

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: applying a kind of residential standard to that hotel necessarily increases the number of violations.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So it's not an indication necessarily of, it's a data point that actually does require a bit more nuance.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Regardless, it is our responsibility and we have the tools to make improvements in those systems.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Also, that data does not, it indicates an issue.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It doesn't indicate which of those have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So on its face, I would say that, you know, like looking at it the way you did, I would say, yes, this is a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We must do something about it.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think we're going to go back with this understanding and kind of understand a little bit more about what's going on there and certainly take additional action if needed to remedy those facilities.

chapters.summary: Morano asks who signs off on continuing to pay for facilities with dozens of violations. Dalton says she is ultimately responsible and will ensure standards are met.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano asks who signs off on paying facilities with violations

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When the city decides to continue paying for a facility with dozens of outstanding violations, who signs off on that decision?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I mean, ultimately, I'm responsible for the system and happy to be responsible for that system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's probably a more technical answer to exactly when that we actually we do that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But as I said, with with more.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Visibility, which I'm glad to have had the opportunity to take a look at that information.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to go in and make sure that they are meeting our standards.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One final question, if I may, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And no doubt that you prefer the two-minute timer to the five-minute timer as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But you report that serious violence inside shelters has been declining, which is great, very encouraging.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to give DHS credit when the numbers show improvement.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There's another question that's important to the people I represent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When you evaluate shelter safety,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you measure only what happens inside the building, or do you also measure what happens in the surrounding community, in the surrounding blocks?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Again, I'm not 100% sure who was in the room at various points, but I mentioned earlier that I spent a good deal of time in preparing for this testimony to integrate all of the NYPD 911.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Data along with our incident reporting.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: system complaint data, not just to look at what was happening inside the shelter system, but to look at the surrounding area, particularly as we open new shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so as soon, and I'm very anxious to do this, no matter what it says, it's important to know, as soon as we can get that data fully aligned so that we're certain it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We'll do that analysis.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I had done it, but we just have some concerns about the way it's been integrated, and I can't be confident in the results.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right, but you'll get it to us when you can.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, it's a really important analysis, and it has to be done with care.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And other people should check our work so that you can see it being independent as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about mental health needs and metrics. Fellini says DHS assesses at intake and revisits program models; Dalton says behavioral health integration is a priority.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions DHS on mental health metrics

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Two quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is on the mental health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know there are bills in the past that say you have to cover mental and physical health in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question on the mental health was, is that is something that you are finding is increasing and how?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What metrics you're using and how you're treating it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's a big issue, I think, elsewhere.

chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions DHS on school transfers and busing

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then secondly, just back to my school situation, when you have a family that has school-age, like we heard earlier about how many

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: ex-caseworkers on housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how many people are helping with school transfer from the shelters?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm a big...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: a win fan that they have, but not everybody has a school person.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how long does it take to get that family into school?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you dealing with the bus situation, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because that's where there's so many problems along the way for these families.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So the mental health and then just how do you get them into school at timing?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the questions.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So when it comes to mental health, we are assessing folks that come in at a particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we know with those living with mental illness, it may present differently depending on the circumstances, especially if these are high-stress situations.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we can get back to you on whether or not the number of people we serve are experiencing mental health issues.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But, again, that would be a point in time, likely at assessment for single adults when they come in.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We continue to revisit our program models to make sure that we are staffing shelters to meet the needs of those residents that are there.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And where we don't have a program model that does, that shelters have a network of community-based organizations to refer folks out to to get the services that they need.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, I'm familiar.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The families seem to have more support, but individuals are pretty wild.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just don't see enough mental.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Illness support in the shelters.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But you're paying more attention to that?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Oh, God.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're nuts.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: is a particular area of interest for me, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we're looking at different models to ensure that people in our shelter system, and certainly there are a lot of single adults in the system who don't have significant behavioral health needs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But there is a group.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This is something we're looking at addressing in the homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But it's just hard on the ones who are doing really well to be in the same space of the ones who aren't.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, we're looking at improvements as we work on the homelessness plan.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We think there are certainly models of care that can get.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Behavioral health care for anyone who needs it into the system and not just behavioral health care, but also, you know, for looking at kids with asthma, making sure that they're getting like, you know, regular conditions as medical needs met.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think there is a lot more we can do in integrating these two systems of care so that people are in fact getting the care, the medication management and the support that they need.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And if I may, I was just actually looking for the number.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I told you it is also something that we are working actively with our partners in the school system on.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Cleaning up data to make sure we actually know the transport routes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I was looking for the number of people who are currently assigned to be kind of case managers on that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On school issues.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On school issues.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we're looking at that with the school system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's not one for every shelter, but some of those folks cover multiple shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But just looking at the ways we can use those resources better, again, our own staff doing door knocking where kids are missing school

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and ensuring that the transportation data is both correct so we know where kids and families are supposed to be going, as well as we're addressing those needs faster.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So operationally, we are very much on this and agree it's a critically important issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, just with the buses letting go, you've got to call Kevin Moran because everybody else, forget it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been on with him all day.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He's in charge of buses.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So your caseworker better have his cell number.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to call Kevin Moran.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: It's holding right now, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilor Brewer.

chapters.summary: Aviles asks how whistleblower policies are communicated to staff and subcontractors and how many complaints there have been. Dalton says she does not have the information and will follow up.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles questions DHS on whistleblower policies

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Councilor Brewer-Viles.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés

chapters.summary: Aviles asks how shelter residents are protected from retaliation and whether DHS tracks complaints from subcontractors. Fellini says DHS investigates retaliation and does not carve out subcontractor complaints but can look into it.
chapters.title: Council Member Aviles questions DHS on resident retaliation protections and subcontractor complaints

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And also, I'd love to know how shelter residents are.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Obviously, we know there's an ombudsman, but how they receive that and how they are protected against retaliation, potentially from staff.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I will say I'm concerned that while I understand it theoretically,

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: that the subcontractors obviously should report back up to their main provider.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: But if there is no way, I'd be curious, number one, how many complaints you've received from subcontractors.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Do we have a naughty list?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Are we seeing providers use the same contractors over and over again?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I'd love to hear more about how we're closing that loop because there is a potential for real problems there.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We don't have data on complaints to from subcontractors or about subcontractors specifically carved out in the data, but we can certainly look into that because I think you're raising an important point.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: When it comes to retaliation, obviously this is of utmost concern as we're trying to create a safe and welcoming environment.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Where staff and clients both feel that they can be safe.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So if we are to hear about an instance of retaliation, obviously we're going to investigate.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We want to understand what the provider knows, what they've done about this, and who the bad actor is.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And if the findings warrant it, may lead to termination.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So we're looking into every aspect of the provider's handling of the particular issue, as well as is there something underlying this, right?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Was the bad actor permitted by LAX Pro?

utterances.text: to calls to be able to do this.

utterances.text: So we're looking to make sure that supervision is right, that security is right.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah, and see if it's spread.
