chapters.title: Council Member Aviles requests packet on resident rights and language access

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, and I guess I'd be interested certainly to see what the kind of assessment is, certainly across and the communication of the policy to staff and to subcontractors as well.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I guess I just would love to underscore the importance of, I think you mentioned earlier that you don't track the, I guess, language accessibility of providers, although...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I would imagine that they understand the population that they are requesting to service.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: However, I have seen a good number of providers who have no language competency at all.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And so would love to see a more digging deep of a requirement rather than a suggestion or an expectation that they may follow it with no way of being able to hold account.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And we are able to track their use of the language line, but I understand the concern is more about having real people on site that can speak in the language of the client that's in front of them.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And in terms of just to go back to how does DHS investigate whistleblower complaints, if you could, for the record?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And in terms of whistleblower protection policies only apply to vendors, employees, and contractors.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: And I guess, as I mentioned earlier, shelter residents should be protected against retaliation for filing complaints about the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: How are these rights and protections communicated to shelter residents?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There's a whole series of documents somebody receives when they come into shelter and their rights and responsibilities, the grievance process, the ability to be treated fairly and with respect are all codified in those materials.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's also part of what happens during routine case management, during the grievance investigation, incidents.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So there are multiple ways that it's communicated.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be really helpful if the agency could provide to the council offices, let's say we have multiple facilities, a packet that includes

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: what that process and procedure is, a packet that includes what the good neighbor policy is.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: I remember chasing that down for years on end.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And if I may add, just because it is such an important issue of people feeling safe from retaliation when they're making complaints, and we heard from the panel who opened up this session that they felt, at least one person had felt that they had

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: been retaliated upon or they were concerned about reporting for fear of retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I haven't just heard that today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I do hear that with some frequency.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And it is why, in addition to the ways that we're kind of required to have a complaint process and handle it, that direct communication,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: regular communication through technology, text messaging, and so on, can help me and this team understand directly from people what

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: what's impacting them so that we may take that into account along with other measures.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that is something that is important to me to build out.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Yeah, no, and I think certainly our council offices will, of course, reach out to you directly, but I think as a proactive measure, it would be...

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Really great to be able to offer your council representatives a packet of information that they should readily know, both for staff, for residents, for contractors, because the truth is we will get

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: all of the above coming to our offices and to help them better navigate the situation.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: That would be quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DHS handles resident conflict. Fellini says there is no formal mediation process; providers handle conflict, may move residents within a building, or transfer to another shelter.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on conflict mediation between residents

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: All right, you're going to get me in trouble with Councilmember Murano taking up so much time.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: He's not here, Chair, so you get to do what you want.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for your questions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, how does DHS handle conflict between shelter residents, and is there a mediation process?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: formal mediation process that DHS issues, but we look to our providers to handle conflict on site, and that can happen in a few ways.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So I mentioned Local Law 49 and our customer service training, which is not just about how to provide good service.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's about how to interact with clients, with staff, to make sure that everybody feels that they are being treated with respect, that they feel safe.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: In instances where conflict seems to not be able to be resolved through the efforts of the provider,

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: it's possible that we might, the provider might decide to move the client or the household to another side of the building if we're meeting in the hallway and there are issues there.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If things escalate in consultation with the DHS program staff, we might choose to transfer that household to a different shelter.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: But there's different levels of engagement that DHS has.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We really look to our providers to implement mediation, trauma-informed approach to the work that they do every day.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And de-escalation security training.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about training on sanctuary city policies and ICE entering shelters. Fellini says DHS has required trainings and refreshers. Dalton says ICE incidents are reviewed and lessons shared with providers.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on sanctuary city training and ICE incidents

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Last year, there were reports that ICE had entered DHS shelters without judicial warrants in violation of the city's sanctuary city laws.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What training does DHS give staff in relation to DHS policies in general and sanctuary city policies?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Specifically and how frequently does that training take place?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I know it's one thing to have the policies written down in the books somewhere that people read maybe some years ago, but how frequently are you reminding people what the policies are?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We have quite a number of trainings that are required across the system, and we do have refreshers both internally, and we require the provider to be refreshing with their own staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think in addition to the book of policies and saying everybody was trained, in the moment at 2 o'clock in the morning, it might all go out the window.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: So this is also about how we're implementing this in real time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And sorry, do you track?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Compliance or efficiency in terms of the providers giving the training or refreshing their training?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We track refreshers, yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Not with me, no.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I would add, and I believe this to be true, but we can confirm, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: whenever there's been an incident.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: with ICE at any of our DHS shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We take that very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our council gets involved.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We review what happened in that case.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We deal with it as it's happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's a direct number to call to us to get advice as needed.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then I think we have been pretty good at sharing lessons from each of those individual incidents and communicating them to providers because things are changing in the ways that

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This has happened over the period.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I think we've been in really good communication with our provider network about what to do, how to do it, in addition to the kind of more formal trainings.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on security budget and expenditures

utterances.text: DHS's total security budget for fiscal 2026 as of the fiscal 2027 adopted plan is $313 million.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How much was actually spent in fiscal 2026?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We think we have that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We're looking for it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Give us just one second.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You need to take a section.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And while you're looking for what was spent in fiscal 2026, I would love to also know the total security budget for fiscal 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We're looking now.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We may have to get back to you on both of those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But if we find them during the hearing, we'll certainly report back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: My computer is dying, and I would really like to, at some point, testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm a shelter resident, and I submitted...

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We will be getting to the public testimony in just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think we have something that's responsive to your question, Chair Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Although I'm not 100% sure I remember the question, but I can read an answer.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The total security budget for fiscal 2026 as of...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Fiscal 2027 adopted plan was reported as $313 million.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I'm wondering for fiscal 2026, how much of that $313 million was actually spent?

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how the FY27 amount was determined and funding sources. Priester says most is city tax, PS lines, contracted security, equipment, and body-worn camera contracts; DHS will provide a breakdown.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about FY27 security budget breakdown and funding sources

utterances.text: Our numbers are quite different.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So why don't we...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Well, why don't you give me the numbers that you have?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The number we have is for DHS peace officers is 18 million and contracted security is 40.8 million.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that's very different than, so it must be counting perhaps across DSS and we're answering for DHS here.

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Peace officers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But we're happy to clarify as needed.

utterances.text: Yes, that could be an error on my part.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Well, I would love to know.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have the total security budget for fiscal 2027?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Were those the numbers for 26?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Those are for 27, for FY27.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I would love to also know the numbers for FY26, if and when you have those.

utterances.text: We don't have those here, but we can give you a bit of a trend.

utterances.text: If you have a funding breakdown, so you mentioned equipment, contract and security, peace officers.

utterances.text: We have body-worn cameras, so our evidence.com contract and any of our other equipment contracts, and we can provide that breakdown.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It would be great if you all can follow up with that.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about theft and lockable storage. Fellini says single adult shelters must provide lockable storage and can store valuables. Priester says security risk assessments check that lockers are not movable.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on theft and securing personal belongings

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, we've heard concerns about theft of personal belongings in shelters, seemingly due to a lack of space to lock belongings away.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is your policy for bringing in and securing personal belongings into shelters?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: As per state regs in single adult shelters, we are required to provide lockable storage and the client is given the key or the code.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It's for them to use to keep their belongings secured.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: If they choose, we can also store valuables for a client as long as they need to.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: On site?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: On site.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Small articles of jewelry perhaps or documents, money orders.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the area that they're given a key to lock away their own belongings?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What type of space are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It depends on the site.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The facility, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Assuming it's a single adult congregate site, it's usually the storage cabinet that separates beds.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what does DHS do to prevent and address theft in shelters?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Again, ensuring that locks are kept secured, that if we see damage, if clients are reporting damage, that we're responsive to that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Priester can also speak to security in the facilities and their role in making sure that clients'belongings are kept secured and to prevent theft.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I don't want to give anybody any ideas, but I'm just trying to envision or imagine the size of those lockers, let's call them.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can one lift that up and remove it?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: That's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: The ones that are directly runs and most of the provider facilities, no.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So when my team does security risk assessments, that's one of the biggest things that we look at to make sure that they're not movable.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But was there anything you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Just in regards to the death, one of the things that we do when the providers document the complaints, we do take steps to try to locate the belongings, including speaking with staff, reviewing surveillance footage, and if it's appropriate, contact the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how DHS supports CPAP machines, oxygen tanks, and refrigerated medication. Fellini says DHS ensures appropriate outlets, access control, and provides refrigeration or mini fridges.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on medical devices and medication storage

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How does DHS support people who require medical devices, including mobility aids and items that require electricity or batteries like CPAP machines, personal ECG or EKG monitors, oxygen tanks, and diabetes monitors?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How do you assist people in keeping these items safe and functional?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yeah, I think in the same way that Deputy Commissioner Priester shared, making sure that these, first of all, that these devices, that we're aware of them,

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: especially for things that need to be plugged in, that they're in an appropriate outlet, and that if they are not on the person, that we're making sure we're keeping eyes

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: and ensuring also, I think, through access control, making sure that people are coming in and out only with their belongings.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what about medications that require refrigerators or refrigeration?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: We provide refrigeration.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Clients can, especially in family and adult family shelters, have access to mini fridges.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Same can, we will store for single adults medication that requires refrigeration.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about projections for people leaving Rikers. Dalton says the administration is convening partners to provide direct shelter access and avoid traditional intake, and to connect people to benefits and behavioral health care.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on Rikers closure and shelter planning

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a few questions related to Riker's closure.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And planning for that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: As the city moves toward closing Rikers Island, what projections has the administration developed regarding the number of individuals who will require transitional housing or shelter placements upon release, and what specific housing capacity is being developed to meet that demand?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't know if I can answer that question specifically, but the administration is convening all government partners to think about how we are executing on the closed Rikers plan, including looking at

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: efforts to ensure that people who are coming out of Rikers who don't have any other place to stay have more direct access to our shelter system so that they need not go

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: through intake and assessment after they've been in essentially an intake and assessment facility for some time, that we can do that directly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And looking at the kinds of programming that people need to be successful, whether that be access, as much as we can do to get people's access to benefits.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Restarted as they exit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Anything from that to making sure they have proper behavioral health care.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And again, to obviously the key component with us is making sure that they can get into the housing system that will work for them.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Speaking my language, that sounds as close to auto-enrollment as one could perhaps get.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I support that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about formal planning with Mach J and data on exits to shelter. Dalton says she will follow up on specifics and notes significant overlap between the Rikers population and homelessness.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about formal planning with Mach J and data on Rikers exits

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What formal planning process exists between DHS and Mach J to ensure that people leaving Rikers do not enter the traditional shelter system unnecessarily?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And which agency is responsible for leading that work?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I know you just touched on...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But is there a formal, it sounds like it's the full.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: administration is bringing everybody to the table, but are you all working directly with Mach J and who ultimately is responsible?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I may look to my colleagues for specifics here and or need to get back to you on the specifics of how that's working on the ground, because I know that's what's important to people.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It doesn't matter if I meet with the commissioner or we meet at this level to ensure what matters is what happens on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I will probably have to get back to you with those specifics.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But as I said, there's, I think, good work happening, which is reform work.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't think today, I don't think in the past, the recent past, it was the case that people wouldn't just be released and have to go through our traditional shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think it is innovation reform work that's happening to ensure that that handoff is happening and that assessment is done prior to exit from incarceration so that people may get into stable housing quickly and effectively.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are you able to provide data on how many individuals exiting custody enter DHS shelters and how many are connected to transitional housing programs

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: and what performance metrics are being used to evaluate whether the city's housing strategy is supporting the successful closure of Rikers?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I certainly do not have that right now.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I have, we are, as an administration, we are looking.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: at that data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And there is a significant overlap between people who are in Rikers today or are leaving Rikers who have previous homelessness experience.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so it is a critical connection and we can probably work with other partners to provide that information.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for those answers.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites Local Law 124 requiring 40 hours of training and an 8-hour refresher. Priester says there are 3,542 security guard positions as of September 1, 2026.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on security guard training and vacancies

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, moving into staff and training.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Local Law 124 of 2021 requires security guards and DHS shelters to receive an additional 40 hours of training within 120 days of hiring

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: and an annual eight-hour refresher training of which at least two hours must be techniques for interactions with individuals experiencing homelessness and individuals in a mental health emergency or crisis.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How many security guard positions are there in shelters?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: As of our September 1st, 2026 reporting period, there was 3,542.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks vacancy rates. Priester says DHS does not track aggregate security guard vacancy; the peace officer vacancy rate is 20%.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about security guard and peace officer vacancy rates

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the current vacancy rate for shelter security guards?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So that is not something that we track as an aggregate.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: However, so as we've kind of discussed, there's the DHS peace officers, and we can provide information there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then there's the provider system that contracts with security.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that's a moving target.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't think it would be easy for us to ever give you a good number on that figure.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But Deputy Commissioner can report on DHS peace officers.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites a 2024 report on misconduct involving 31 peace officers. Priester says 18 shelters have peace officers, staffing ranges from 10 to 26, and they receive academy training on use of force, de-escalation, and crisis intervention.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on peace officer misconduct and training

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In 2024, New York State Focus released a report about misconduct among peace officers and shelters and cited disciplinary incidents involving 31 officers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Some of these incidents included the use of excessive physical force against shelter residents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How many shelters have peace officers?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that DHS has 352.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Peace officers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Well, I think the commissioner did in her testimony, not you specifically, but 352 peace officers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So how many shelters have peace officers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 18 shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And how many peace officers are assigned to a shelter and how is that determination made?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So staffing ranges from 10 to 26.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you just pull the microphone closer?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Staffing ranges from 10 to 26 peace officers in the shelters that have the HS police.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: We determine those assignments based on the level of police presence needed to support each site's daily operational needs and security risks.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: This may be a little redundant, so forgive me if it is, but what training do peace officers who work in DHS shelters receive?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And is this different than the training given to security guards?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So DHS peace officers receive comprehensive training through our DCJES-approved police training academy,

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: but training programs that have also been evaluated and recognized by the National College Credit Recommendation Service with initial peace officer training recommended for 10 college clients.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Reflecting the depth and rigor of the curriculum, which is different than the training given to security guards.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Training begins with an issue peace officer instruction and continues throughout an officer's career through in-service training and annual certification requirements.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: The curriculum covers law enforcement procedures, appropriate use of force, defensive tactics, crisis intervention, de-escalation, conflict resolution, and emergency response.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Beyond the technical aspects of law enforcement, we place significant emphasis on communication.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Sound judgment, and understanding the unique needs of the individuals we serve.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: We also continuously review and expand our training curriculum to reflect the evolving needs of our shelter populations, reinforce professional standards, and strengthen how officers respond to challenging situations.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Our expectation is that every officer understands not only the authority they have, but the responsibility that comes with exercising that authority appropriately, professionally, and with respect for the people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is DHS's process for reviewing and dealing with complaints against peace officers in shelters?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So all complaints received for DHS peace officers are routed to our DSS legal and our DSS special investigation division for appropriate review and action.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks current staff-to-resident ratios. Fellini provides model budget staffing for 200-bed shelters: 43 for single adults, 46 with behavioral health, 51 at assessment, 60 for adult families, and 37 for families with children.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on staff-to-resident ratios

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We understand that there are often many staff vacancies at shelters and turnover rates are high.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is the current staff to resident ratio in shelter?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.text: Based on the model budgets that I mentioned before, where each shelter type has their own model budget, we adjusted to a certain capacity level, 200, so I can read off by program type

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: what we would expect for a shelter with a capacity of 200.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: For single adults, 43 staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: For single adults with behavioral health services, 46 staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: For single adult employment, 43 staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: At our single adult assessment sites, 51 staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: For our adult family shelters, 60 staff.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And for our family with children shelters, 37 staff.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And if I could clarify, that's just PS lines.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are some contracted staff that would not be accounted for in these lines.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, but I would presume then that that would make an even better ratio.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, what is the ideal staff-to-resident ratio?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is it what you listed?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: I think it depends on the program, and it depends on the needs of the clients, and it's something we're continually assessing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So these numbers change?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: The numbers change.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: And again, the model budget is the model.

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: There are times where when the provider demonstrates a need for increased staff, we can go to OMB and request an increase.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And the numbers you gave me are based on the model budget?

utterances.speaker: Christine Clarke
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what DHS does to retain staff. Priester describes succession planning, recognition, men's and women's conferences, exit interviews, and placing new officers near their homes.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on staff retention and vacancies

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And, okay, I know you just mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, but what is DHS doing to fill vacancies and help staff stay in their roles?

utterances.text: You don't have to go into the fill vacancies because I know you're working on filling the vacancies, but what are you doing to help keep people in the room?

utterances.text: So, yes, we have a whole retention process that we're working on with our officers.

utterances.text: One of those processes is really looking at succession planning and trying to see how officers would like to make their...

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Complete their career with DHS and what career advancement looks like.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: One of the other things that we are doing is we have instituted a men's conference, a women's conference, where we're working with the officers to kind of understand and hear ideas around how we can work to make things better for them.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I think I'm echoing the commissioner's sentiments to say that I don't think any of those things are arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I think those are very intentional ways to maintain or increase retention.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would just suggest other sort of affinity groups.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes, beyond such gendered roles.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: And we're saying men's conference, women's conference as a whole, but we're always looking to just kind of make sure that we're looking to kind of recognize our officers and the hard work that they do on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: One of the other things that we are doing is we do make sure that when people do leave interview and try to understand what that is and

utterances.text: being meaningful and planning full around trying to change the narrative.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: One of the other things that has happened in the past is officers tend to be able to not, I'm sorry, let me correct that.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: One of the things that has happened in the past is officers wasn't allowed to transfer

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: immediately after coming into our academy.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: And we have been really meaningful around making sure that we place officers in their above-road residence, which has increased...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Meaning they couldn't transfer sites.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: They couldn't transfer sites that they're just in, they're new, they're going to get whatever schedule that comes to them.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Like a seniority thing?

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: So we still practice seniority.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: We absolutely have to.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: But what we do do is as officers coming out of the academy, we recognize that anybody that scored as a highest, that we place them at the site that they want to be in.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: And then in rank order, we start placing them in the above-road preference.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, that's great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then...

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how salaries compare to other agencies. Priester says DHS peace officer salaries are extremely low and competing agencies pay more, causing attrition. Dalton calls it a structural problem involving DCAS and state civil service.

utterances.text: What are, how do the salaries compare to security officers at other agencies?

utterances.text: The salaries for our DHS peace officer is extremely low.

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Some competing agencies actually exceed what the DHS peace officers actually receive, and that is the...

utterances.speaker: Valvunch Priester
utterances.text: Predominant reason on why we're losing offices.

utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So perhaps this is something that...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's important.

utterances.text: It is.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about preventing illness in congregate shelters. DHS says prevention is key, with vaccination reminders, winter coat checks, and single-occupancy isolation rooms.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, large congregate shelters create an increased risk for the spread of infectious disease, especially during cold and flu season.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What measures does DHS take to help prevent the spread of illness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So prevention is key.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we work with our providers to make sure that through routine engagement with the clients that they're serving, that reminders about getting

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: vaccinations, going to the doctor, staying healthy, dressing appropriately if we see somebody leaving the facility without a winter coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: in the winter to make sure that people do not contract a contagious illness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If they were to, we do have single occupancy isolation rooms to keep that from spreading.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites Local Law 35. DHS says 113 of 143 targeted sites, or 79%, have one or more mental health professionals on site who assess families and make referrals.

utterances.text: And then Local Law 35 of 2023 requires DHS to have a mental health professional available in shelters for families with children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.text: And hold on one second.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We understand that DHS uses telehealth in many shelters to comply with Local Law 35.

utterances.text: Are shelter residents utilizing telehealth options?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have to get back to you on the numbers, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe they're in the MMR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And the language of Local Law 35 subjects a requirement of having mental health professionals available in shelters for families with children to appropriations.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: However, we've been told by some providers that DSS has told shelters they must provide mental health services without increasing their budget.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about training to identify serious mental illness and make SPOA referrals. DHS says it collaborates with DOHMH on quarterly mandatory training and coordinates with ACT and SPAC teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Shelter staff are trained in harm reduction and overdose response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN

utterances.text: And staff-client interactions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is required for a complaint to be deemed resolved?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The shelter director must respond with the appropriate next step.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So either they are reporting out that they have done something to resolve, met with the client, followed up with a landlord on a housing package, or what they're going to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm going to meet with the client and report back to DHS about the interaction.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the average number of days from receiving a complaint to its resolution?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Five days.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what counts as resolved and average days. DHS says the shelter director must respond with the next step, average resolution is five days. DHS says it does not incorporate complaint data into provider performance evaluations or RFP scores.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DHS on complaint resolution and provider evaluations

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Does DHS review and incorporate data about complaints and provider performance evaluations or RFP proposal scores?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, and then I think it was the commissioner who said the data you collect, or maybe it was you, Deputy Commissioner, apologies, I don't remember who it was specifically, but the data you collect on the placement of families, this is in regards to Intro 99.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The data you collect on the placement of families with children is by borough, but boroughs are very large.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Would it not be more useful to collect zip code level data as contemplated by this bill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think the bill does two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The bill changes the geography at which the data is reported, but it also changes the data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we would be interested in the course of working with council and the sponsor on both pieces of that, but I think...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Having coherence in the actual measure is important to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think we would prefer to keep the measure that's in the mayor's management report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But if a lower level of geography is, but I guess that doesn't work because we're reporting on the school district of the last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you understand what the current MMR is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At the end of the day, yes, we collect these data, and I think I did respond to that,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and understand, I think, what the council is trying to do and understand this better, but just some additional dialogue, I think, about

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: making sure that we're not running at different measures and also reporting at a level of geography and specificity that is helpful to the public.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all very much for your testimony and all of your answers to our questions.

chapters.summary: Wilkie, Coalition for the Homeless, says shelters are chaotic due to staff mistreatment, unresponsive complaints, and poor conditions. She says 31,000 complaints undercount because evening and weekend complaints go to 311 and are not reported to the ombudsman.
chapters.title: Allison Wilkie testifies on shelter mistreatment and complaint gaps

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So my name is Allison Milkey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Government Affairs and Strategic Campaigns at the Coalition for the Homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So as the court and city pointed monitors of the DHS shelter system, we receive and investigate complaints from shelter residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Our monitors are in shelters every day, and we provide services to folks in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: And the experiences that we hear from residents is that shelters are chaotic, they are stressful,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: and it's really a direct product of the mistreatment that they experience from staff, the lack of responsiveness from system actors to complaints, the physical conditions that folks endure, and the overall inability people have to get their needs met.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: There's significant ways in which DHS is failing on all of these fronts, and I want to give you just like a quick list of some of these things and some color maybe to what we heard from DHS today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So I think mistreatment and abuse by staff is prevalent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: We get twice as many complaints to our shelter monitoring hotline about that than we do about safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: On a daily basis, people have to interact with the lowest paid and lowest trained staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So in the majority of shelters, case managers and supervisors are behind locked doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: And when people need to have their basic needs met, they're interacting with security guards and residential aides who are in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: not trained and often escalate conflict for people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: I think a second point that we see a lot is their responses to complaints and grievances being inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: I think we just heard that in calendar year 25 or 26, there were over 31,000 complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: But under DHS's policy, if something is not considered an urgent building complaint or not considered a serious complaint, so if it falls into this other category,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: It only goes to the ombudsman's office if the complaint is made from Monday through Friday from 9 to 5.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Everything happening in the evenings and weekends gets referred to 311, and DHS's policy says that 311 specifically does not tell the ombudsman's office about those complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So I think 31,000, which should be a really concerning number to us, is actually a vast miscount of the complaints that people are calling about to various actors.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So just to clarify, sorry, that 31,000 number you're saying implies only complaints made to the ombudsman Monday through Friday, 9 to 5?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Yeah, for other complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: If they're not like urgent, serious complaints, anything that they categorize as other goes to 311 and doesn't go back to the ombudsman's office under their policy.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: So I know my time is up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: I have 11 pages of written testimony that you all have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We will read all 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Allison Wilkie
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Mann, Win, says 40% of families were placed in a different borough than the youngest child's school. He supports Intro 99 for zip code data and urges passage of Intro 816 and Intro 232 to fix PATH intake.
chapters.title: Chris Mann testifies on family shelter placements and Intro 99

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hudson and the rest of the committee for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: I also want to say thank you to the commissioner for staying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: I feel like that's unusual, which is nice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: I'm Chris Mann.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: I'm the vice president of public policy and strategy at Wynn, the largest provider of shelter and supportive housing for families with children in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Each night, nearly 7,000 people call Wynn home, including 3,800 children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Homelessness is traumatic and causes long-term educational damage for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Last year, approximately 40% of families were placed in a different borough than their youngest child's school, forcing children to endure long commutes just to get to class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: The city has to set a higher standard to ensure students experiencing homelessness have the same access to educational continuity as their house peers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: That's why Intro 99, which when proudly crafted in partnership with Councilmember Gail Brewer, is so vital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: For the first time, it will track true community displacement, measuring placements by zip code,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: giving us the precise data needed to understand the gap between where families lived before entering shelter and where they live when they're in the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: The human toll is also painfully evident at path intake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Families face a grueling verification process that takes 53 days on average, five times longer than it should, leaving parents and children feeling deterred and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: sometimes forced back into unsafe and abusive living conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: While not being heard today, we urge the Council to prioritize fixing the broken intake system at PATH and pass Intro 816, sponsored by Council Member Barrios, and Intro 232, sponsored by you, Chair Hudson, in addition to passing Intro 99.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Intro 816 allows self-attestation of housing history to end endless denial loops, and Intro 232 shortens the housing history requirement from two years to one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: I urge the Council to pass these three bills to protect families and end this compounding trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Mann
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Berkman, NYLAG, says the city fails to oversee shelters and safety transfers often require legal intervention. She supports Intro 99 to keep families near their communities and schools.
chapters.title: Deborah Berkman testifies on safety transfers and shelter oversight

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Chair Hudson and staff, good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: My name is Deb Berkman, and I am the director of the Shelter and Economic Stability Project at New York Legal Assistance Group, or NILAG.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: At NILAG, we represent New Yorkers who are trying to access shelter, who are living in shelter, and who are navigating public benefit systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Through that work, I hear every day from people experiencing homelessness about what it is actually like to live in our shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Based on our experience, one of the biggest barriers to safety and shelter is the city's failure to adequately oversee the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Too often, there's no meaningful way to address unsafe conditions, staff misconduct, theft, harassment, or retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And as a result, people are forced to endure unsafe situations with little hope that anyone will intervene or they will be forced into the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: But a particularly significant problem is the difficulty to our clients of obtaining what was called a safety transfer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And I know Commissioner Dalton testified a little bit about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: When a placement becomes unsafe, if someone experiences threats, harassment, theft, violence, or other dangerous conditions in shelter, they should be able to move to a safer placement, but too often they can't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: In practice, many safety transfers are only approved after legal intervention, but even we encounter opposition when we're advocating for our clients for a safety transfer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And many of our clients have been forced into street homelessness rather than remain in shelter where they're just not safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Just as importantly, there doesn't seem to be an effective process for investigating and adjudicating complaints of safety issues in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: The city must provide stronger oversight and meaningful accountability for shelter providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And without that accountability, the unsafe conditions and mistreatment will continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: We strongly support Intro 99.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Families should be housed as close as possible to the homes and communities from which they were displaced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And children should be able to stay connected to their school support system and medical providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: We have written testimony as well, which we will submit, but thank you very much for your time and your attention to these matters.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks whether Berkman contacts site staff or DHS. Berkman says she contacts DHS legal, but clients have already tried at the shelter and been denied or ignored. Hudson says lawyers should not be needed for safety transfers.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions Deborah Berkman on safety transfer process

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I just want to ask, when you've advocated on behalf of clients, is that like directly with the security officers or management at the site, or is it with DHS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: So I generally will contact DHS legal because I'm a lawyer and the people on my team work with DHS legal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And there is still at times opposition when we bring up a safety request.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I mean, so you're an attorney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, don't take offense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But just because I feel like lawyers talking to lawyers is always going to be a little...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: You shouldn't need a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Challenging.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You shouldn't need a lawyer, and I totally support that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But I just wonder if the lawyers are saying something that could be maybe a little bit different from what...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: other folks in DHS could potentially say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Right, what programs would say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: What I will say is that we would never request a safety transfer for a client unless they had already requested it themselves and not gotten anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: So 100% of our safety transfer requests, the clients have already tried.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: To bring it up at their shelter and it hasn't been denied.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: It's been denied or it hasn't been processed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I guess also what I'm, the point that I'm trying to make is, and probably not in the best or most articulate way, is the lawyers probably shouldn't be the people making the decision or determination as to whether or not somebody should be

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: moved for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: And if someone feels unsafe, then there is a safety threat.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Flores says he has reported crimes at BRC, Bellevue, and Breaking Ground shelters for over a decade, including assaults, larceny, corruption, and fraud. He calls for federal hearings and indictments.
chapters.title: Richard Flores testifies on crime and corruption in shelters

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Flores, I believe, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: We've spoken before in previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: Chair Hudson, I've reported incident reports to the NYPD, Department of Inspection, Internal Affairs Bureau, and CCRB regarding crime occurring at city shelters, facilities, and now a safe haven for over a decade to this committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: The Bowie Residence Committee, Bellevue Hospital Men's Shelter, and Breaking Ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: So that's two not-for-profit organizations and one city-run shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: The crimes that I reported ranged from sexual and physical assaults, grand and petty larceny,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: namely corruption and fraud, which if an official, I believe, federal government investigation were held today,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: indictments and prosecutions involving numerous public officials as well as private citizens, I believe would be imprisoned for the crimes that they've committed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: For over, pardon me, for over...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: A decade, I have witnessed recidivist offenders go unpunished by the United States city, state, federal, and judicial system as a result of past and present legislation that was passed by the United States Congress, the House of Representatives, and the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: In this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: With regard to the general welfare and public safety, administration after administration that I've witnessed are failing the city of New York and its citizens in a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: which can only be defined, I believe, as irreparable insofar as the human condition is concerned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: I hope that's not too broad for everyone here, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: Dalton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: American citizens have been reduced to existing as dependents and liabilities to a government in which, for many, hundreds and thousands, I believe, feels more like a totalitarian nightmare reality for these individuals, including myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: An amendment to the administrative code requiring reporting on crime statistics at this point in the legislative body, I feel, should be followed up with federal hearings in Washington, D.C., in which I believe indictments and prosecutions would be held

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: in the United States House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Flores
utterances.text: And that's how I feel personally as a person who's been living in the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all.

chapters.summary: De Jesus, a shelter resident, says site director Lisa Harris uses abusive and retaliatory tactics, berates case managers, and uses security to intimidate residents. She says there is no real grievance process.
chapters.title: Viviana De Jesus testifies on retaliation at Praxis shelter

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Good evening, Chair Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I want to thank you for the pointed questions that you asked the DHS Commissioner, Commissioner Dalton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: You asked really great questions, and it was very frustrating to sit here for almost two hours and listen to her say that she didn't have answers, that she would get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: It really feels like she thought she was coming to a social networking event and not to a city council member hearing where she actually had to provide data, real hard facts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: There is no grievance process through shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Let me begin by saying that I am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: My name is Luz Viviana de Jesus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I am a 51-year-old woman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I have 20-plus years as a workforce development professional and 10 years as a business owner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I have earned the respect of the maternal reproductive care community in Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I ran a business for eight years in Washington, D.C., providing maternal services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Doula services, birth and postpartum services to the Medicaid population, Black and brown and immigrant women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: And I served.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: the community faithfully through COVID in the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: And here I am today with my daughter, who is a fourth year college student here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: In a shelter at the Praxis West End Housing Initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: CEO is Svane Jorgensen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: This shelter is, the site director is Lisa Harris.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: This woman is employing and continues to this moment to employ abusive retaliatory tactics against compliant

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: DHS and HRA compliant families in compliance who simply are seeking to advocate for our legal rights to transparency and due process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: In August, I was informed by the case management staff there who is overwhelmed, overworked, underpaid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Berated by her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: She is railroading their careers because she uses them to reinforce her tactics at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I have seen two case managers quit at Praxis in my two and a half months there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: We arrived July, June 29th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: So from June 29th, I have seen two

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: And three staff members quit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: A housing coordinator quit and two case managers quit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: And she just hired another one and she berated her for asking me how I was doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: and how my housing situation was going, berated her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Ganged up on her with her CM supervisor and my previous CM, Charlene Lloyd.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I submitted a five-page testimony on this and the entire thing that's going on there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: She uses her security staff to reinforce her retaliatory and abusive tactics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: They don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I promise you that security staff doesn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: They have families too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: And she uses them to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Your time has expired.

utterances.text: Are you able to submit written testimony, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: DeJesus?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Viviana De Jesus
utterances.text: I submitted written testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: We will review the written testimony.

utterances.text: I just want to...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.
