chapters.summary: Jimenez says he tried for five months to file a grievance but could not get an email address and faced tactical avoidance. He says contracts and performance reviews create incentives to suppress grievances and calls for more social workers.
chapters.title: Jorge Jimenez testifies on grievance process loopholes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm here to support 307.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I consider it extremely important, but I think there's a point that is being restated every time we talk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: It's the fact that the majority of the issues that are affecting people

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: are usually related to grievances that cannot be reported.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: There's actually a lot of conversation about huge words like homicide, rape, grand larceny, or theft, or things like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: But mainly, one of the problems that we're experiencing is that there's some sort of tactical avoidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And plausible deniability that can be created when a process of grievances is not well established.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: That's why I feel, and actually I'm going through a process like that right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I've been trying to report a grievance for the past five months, and I have actually followed the specific hierarchy of things that I had to do with the specific

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: children provider, in this case, a drop-in center provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And pretty much what I've done, it leads to nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I keep entering a loophole that is full of tactical avoidance, implosible deniability, and then there's some specific little tricks that happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: One of them being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: You have to send us an email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: But how can I send you an email to start the process if your staff never provides emails, email addresses to contact them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I cannot start the process if you don't provide me with that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is there not a general email address or line to submit grievances?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Pretty much what you must do is try to guess.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Guess the first letter of the worker, the last name, and then you put at whatever organization you're with, and maybe that becomes...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: The way you deal with that trick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: That's one of the tricks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: There's another one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: The other trick is the let's have a conversation about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Well, the conversations cannot be tracked down because it disappears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: It becomes a conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: There are other tricks that happen, and these are usually correlated to one specific thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: These are contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And these contracts have to be reviewed every year for performance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: A huge amount of grievances can actually lead to a decrease in the qualification that they receive every year, from excellent to good to average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Some of these contracts are for like millions of dollars over five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Too many complaints, let's not use the word complaint, too many grievances, reports can lead to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: We're forgetting two aspects, the business aspect of this part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And another aspect that we're forgetting is the human factor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: One central position, one central type of professional that we're missing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: of the social worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: We don't need more case managers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: That's an euphemism that is being used financially in order to avoid hiring social workers that have been trained to deal with this multiplicity of issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: But social workers are expensive.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For the complaints or grievances that you've submitted, are you saying that you've not received any sort of formal response?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: It was impossible for me to start the process because I did not have the email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Then I found the email through a process.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But there's no like box or anything on site where you can just submit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And then what happened is I actually found the email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: I sent an email to the case manager, but that case manager never answered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: So that's the other trick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: If they don't answer, there is no continuity of service in order to establish a bridge that will actually lead to a proper grievances report.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: And it's premeditated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We'll follow up with you directly as well.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Napier spent 224 days in DHS shelters. She describes a ceiling collapse at Franklin, injury during evacuation, sleeping in wet rooms, no potable water or hot water at Empower, lost medication, and staff retaliation.
chapters.title: Lauren Napier testifies on shelter conditions and staff incompetence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Ready?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Deborah Berkman
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Okay, my name is Lauren Napier, and I want to say, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: DeJesus, I am on par with her as an individual who is a professional who has found herself in the shelter environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I spent 224 days in a DHS shelter, four nights at the Franklin Women's Shelter in the Bronx, and then I resided for the remaining 200 days at the Empower Women's Shelter, which is in Gail Brewer's district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And I am disappointed that she's gone because I would like to have addressed her personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I have gone to her office and communicated with her office on a multitude of occasions and was not helped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I also previously testified at the COGE hearing on June 9th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: But as I said, I was able to exit the shelter within 22, after residing there for 224 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: After and despite 100 days of staff incompetence, staff ignorance, and staff retaliation, egregious levels of staff retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: But first, I want to talk about Franklin because I entered that shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There was a ceiling collapse in that shelter where a water tower came down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Upon evacuation, it was completely chaotic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I actually fell down a flight of stairs, tore my meniscus, and herniated a disc in my back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There was absolutely no level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: of urgency, security, or concern for people's well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And that night, upon having to return to Franklin, we were required to sleep in wet rooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: The room was wet, saturated, so much water that the tiles from the ground were raised, and we were required to sleep in that room.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And sorry, this incident occurred when?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: November 15th, 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I then was moved to the Empower Women's Shelter on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: It is considered a MICA shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: That is a mentally ill, chemically addicted shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: That shelter is inhabited, well, the residents are a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: So you have a mixed population, people like me and people who have severe mental illness and severe disability, along with people who have dementia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: In that shelter, there was not a medical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Any level of medical personnel, not one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: However, there was a box of Narcan that was there for people in the event of an overdose, which I was witness to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: So as our commissioner sat here and discussed the things that happen in the shelter, it is inconsistent with what actually happens inside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And it's really disappointing that it's very clear that there's a cleavage between the information that you have and the real experience that people are experiencing inside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I also experienced and personally was assaulted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I endured.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Months

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: of sleep deprivation, again, hostility from staff, retaliation, even after reporting concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I, like you, sir, completed grievances in writing and in email and were often not responded to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And I then escalated my issues to Jumaane Williams'office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: The Office of the Ombudsman, again back to Gail Brewer, and I, like you, followed the email formats of numerous, numerous city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I followed people on Instagram and DM'd them, sent them messages, all to your offices to no avail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: So I just want to make it clear that you guys are responsible for hundreds of thousands of people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And we are not getting the help that we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: It is an exhaustive effort of individuals who are residing in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: It is exhausting the taxpayer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: We are not, I'm a person who's been on both sides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I'm a taxpayer and I am a person who required and needed the services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And I was not able to effectively get the services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I was doing the job of my case manager, my housing specialist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I too lost an apartment during the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I used my resources to help myself out of the shelter and also to help the people inside of the shelter with me because the staff is unprofessional, unprepared, and ignorant to the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Even so much so that I had to provide them a PDF, a link.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: and language of some of the policies that had been instated that indicate that there is no shelter stay requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: They don't even know the basics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And so to speak about the professionalism and the education of the staff and who's there, it's a farce because that is not what is happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: It's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And I also want to say that the Empower Women's Shelter had no potable drinking water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: We had no hot water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There was another issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: During the Code Blue, no laundry detergent, no hot water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: The staff would hand out bottles of water at their discretion to whom they felt needed water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: They lost people's medication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There was a girl who had her mother's ashes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: They lost the girl's mother's ashes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: When you talk about security and holding people's property, they don't do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: Okay, they're not prepared for...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: individuals'needs, nor do they care about people's needs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I can go on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: There's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have written testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I do have written testimony, and I will provide it in detail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And I would also like the contact information so that we can have a sit-down discussion, because I have sat in one of these hearings, and it's very disappointing also to see our elected officials leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: We sit here, and I understand that they have other constituents, but this is important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And this is an exhaust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: I mean, there's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: ways that the city can save money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: You're hemorrhaging money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: You guys don't even know what the shelters are spending money on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And they're hemorrhaging money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Napier
utterances.text: And they're warehousing people.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We'll follow up.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sir?

chapters.summary: Williams, recently in the DHS system, says New York offers many services but lacks a cookie-cutter transition program. He says he has three grievances he could not turn in due to being directed in circles.
chapters.title: Clifton Williams testifies on lack of communication and grievance access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you press the button?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: My name is Clifton C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: Williams IV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: I'm a recent transplant from the mid-states of America, southern Kentucky, southern Indiana area, back to my hometown of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: And being within this time here, the last 10 and a half months, I have entered into the DHS system

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: just to basically try to see if there is within the compounds of differences within area, region, and even policy and treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: And I will commend New York City on basically a lot of few options because they do offer a myriad of services that many other states have no idea even exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: They are observing the rights of people on an individual basis, even those with special and or mental handicap and or capability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: However, there is no cookie cutter program that's specifically designed to help a person transition from homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: And that's something that I do agree that within the flexibility of these meetings can be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: I did experience a lot of different processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: One of the biggest ones is a lack of communication and an ability to leave grievances and or report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: directly to either the group in hand or with DHS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: I literally have three grievances within my possession back at my shelter that I had intended to turn in on March 3rd.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: And I was directed in so many different directions that, to be honest with you, I figured I entered it back into my appealed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: Court case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: That is the reason why I actually filed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: And it's not because of the fact that I wanted to see any more difficulty implied upon the city, because in all honesty, that is the reason why I came back here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: Because I'm figuring if anyone would be able to show or set up a federal standard within the basic housing needs for a nationwide referendum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: It would be New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clifton C. Williams IV
utterances.text: So hopefully we'll see a resolve within this in the end.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Bruno
utterances.text: And also, thank you for DHS and DSS Commissioner for being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Bruno
utterances.text: My name is Fandi Bruno, and I am the structural coordinator for the Way Alliance Women Experiencing Homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Bruno
utterances.text: I'm a human rights defender under the UN General Assembly Resolution 53144, the Universal Declaration for Human Rights Defenders.

utterances.text: And I'm a victim of severe stalking victimization that stemmed from domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Bruno
utterances.text: And I am at stage eight of the homicide timeline, which is a timeline that was developed by Dr.

chapters.summary: Mercurius, Brooklyn Defender Services, says shelter rules create conflict and staff call law enforcement or ACS. She supports Intro 99 because families are placed far from support networks, causing school absences and ACS risk.
chapters.title: Hannah Mercurius testifies on family shelter placements and school stability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: My name is Hannah Mercurius, and I'm a senior attorney at Brooklyn Defender Services in the civil justice practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: BDS is a public defense office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: We represent about 40,000 people each year in Brooklyn and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Thank you to Councilmember Hudson and the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Our civil justice practice works with people who are entering the shelter system as well as shelter residents attempting to secure stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And as many people have said at this hearing today, shelter residents are subjected to heightened surveillance and are at an increased risk of contact with the criminal and family legal systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Shelters have rigid rules about enter and exit, what residents can eat and wear, who can provide child care for children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And how shelter units must be maintained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: The people we represent share that these stringent requirements often create frequent conflict in shelters and that shelter staff lack training in de-escalation, and they often resort

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: to calling law enforcement and ACS, the Administration for Children's Services, which perpetrates trauma and disruption that shelter residents are already experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And then families are really unlikely to seek support from shelter staff who are the same people who surveil and criticize them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Many of the families who live in shelters have been placed very far away from their existing networks of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: We support Intro 99 in part because we know that families have no control over where they're placed when they enter shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And one of the things that this hearing made me wonder is if families are asked where they want to be placed when they're experiencing intake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: It disrupts the network of supportive people and providers that they've created in their home neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Risking school absences, as we've heard, missed doctor's appointments, and exposing families to ACS investigations during these really precarious transition periods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Even though under the McKinney-Vento Homelessness Assistance Act,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: students in shelter are entitled to transportation to their home, to their schools of origin, we find that there are extensive delays in that busing being put in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And it's unrealistic for parents to travel more than an hour with multiple children to get them to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And as a result, families are often forced to risk that those repeated school absences will incur more surveillance by ACS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Or initiate a case against them if schools call in a report, or make a really impossible decision to change their child's school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: So we support this legislation, and it's more about increasing busing services for families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: It's about ensuring that families experiencing homelessness can access critical systems of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Religious communities, neighbors, schools, stores that they're familiar with, which are essential for families during the incredibly destabilizing experience of entering shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: And we'll submit written testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Strom, Urban Justice Center, says the city must prioritize moving people out of shelter using vacant 9G units, HPD apartments, and 6,000 supportive housing units. She says people languish for years while shelters cost more than vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: We know we have thousands of vacant 9G units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom

utterances.text: There's the right to shelter is incredibly important.

utterances.text: However, we have not done nearly enough to get people out of shelters and into permanent housing.

utterances.text: So many people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: In our group who come to us have been in shelters for years and years and years and years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: And you should not have to be in a shelter for five years or six years or seven years.

utterances.text: It's also not a good use of city resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: To continue to allow people to languish in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: for this amount of time when we do have concrete housing resources in this city is...

utterances.text: It's a choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: And it's a choice that we're making and we need to be putting all of our resources towards getting people out as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: And if you do that and then you have like a smaller number of shelters and people are moving out quickly, then I think that you can have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: A different conversation about like, well, you could actually start closing shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: You could be closing these bad congregate shelters and moving towards just having single rooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: You could be doing very different things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Helen Strom
utterances.text: And I think like that's a really important piece that we hope we can work with the council and get the city to take more action on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Busser, Bronx Defenders, says police presence compounds trauma and Intro 387 risks reinforcing policing. She asks for clear definitions, distinction between allegations and substantiated findings, and separation of resident, staff, and police-response incidents.
chapters.title: Grace Busser testifies on Intro 387 and policing-centered safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: My name is Grace Busser.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: I'm a civil legal advocate in the civil action practice at the Bronx Defenders, a community-oriented public defender that uses an interdisciplinary model

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: comprised of teams of attorneys, social workers, advocates, and others who all collaborate to provide holistic services to our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: The Bronx accounts for almost 40% of all individuals and families entering the New York City shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: It also has the highest concentration of shelters compared to any other borough in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: In my role, I work very closely with the shelter system, advocating for clients to access resources in the hopes that they will transition to stable, healthy, and safe permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: I accompany clients to intake, visit them in shelter, work with shelter workers and case managers to help clients meet their goals and get the services that they need while living there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: So I know that people in shelter are at one of the most vulnerable points in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: They're often entering shelter from traumatizing circumstances, whether living on the streets, recently evicted, released from incarceration, fleeing an unsafe situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Police presence in shelter can compound this trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Residents may avoid reporting victimization if they fear it will bring police further into their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We know that a criminal case can cost a client their shelter placement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: It can jeopardize housing applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: It can affect immigration status and carry collateral consequences for families with children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: More police without stronger services and better living conditions is not the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Those calling shelter their home deserve dignity, support, and safety in a meaningful way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We are concerned that this bill, 387, as written, risks reinforcing a policing-centered approach to shelter safety by emphasizing incident counts and security measures without requiring equivalent transparency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: around staff misconduct, residents'experiences, or the consequences of enforcement decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We have three main concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We need to, one, make the data clear and reliable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Each category of critical incident should be clearly defined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Transparency is crucial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Additionally, the bill does not require DHS to distinguish between allegations and substantiated findings or provide the circumstances surrounding an incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Without these distinctions, the data may present an incomplete or misleading picture of shelter safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Two, we need to measure the impact on residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: I've represented clients whose shelter placements were disrupted following incidents classified by DHS as domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: They've been separated from each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: They've lost their shelter placement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: And while protecting survivors is essential, so is ensuring that DHS appropriately assesses these incidents, understands residents in their own words, and considers the consequences of their response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Three, we need to make staff and security accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Reports should separate incidents between residents from those involving staff or security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: As well as incidents that led to a police response from those that did not.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you provide a little bit more clarity around that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You're saying.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: separate incidents that involved staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: From incidents that involved, say, resident to resident.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: And then additionally, provide reports that separate incidents that resulted in a police response from those that did not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: And then third, separating allegations from substantiated circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We know that without sufficient context, this insufficient reporting can lead to, it can distort comparisons across shelter and across the city, which can reinforce the perception that increased law enforcement involvement is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And with some of those changes, would you be supportive of the legislation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: We would be happy to work with the committee in implementing these changes, and if implemented in a satisfactory way, we might be in support.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Grace Busser
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.text: Is Timothy Pena still here?

utterances.text: Does nobody answer?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If there's anyone present in the room or on Zoom that has not had the opportunity to testify, please raise your hand.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In the room or on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you to everyone who has testified, seeing no one else.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would like to note again that written testimony, which will be reviewed in full by committee staff, may be submitted to the record

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: up to 72 hours after the close of this hearing by emailing testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I think what we have seen here today is not only that, of course, we already know we have so much more work to do in creating safe, secure, and dignified places for people to live who are experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Um

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But we have to prioritize the experiences, the lived experiences of those who are in the shelter system and not just rely on, you know, policies, procedures and laws that exist on the books.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so with that, I just want to thank everybody again for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And with that, I will adjourn today's hearing.

summary: Committee on General Welfare held an oversight hearing on shelter safety and considered Intro 99 on family shelter placements and Intro 387 on critical incident reporting.

DSS Commissioner Erin Dalton and DHS officials testified on security, repairs, data trends, training, grievances, and oversight, facing extensive questions from Council Members Hudson, Morano, Wilson, Brewer, Ung, Nurse, and Aviles.

Public testimony included shelter residents, advocates, and legal service providers describing unsafe conditions, retaliation, grievance barriers, and support for housing-first and transparency measures.
